feat(egress-proxy): workspace-prefixed, owner-keyed policy layout (dual-read) (#28652)

First phase of the egress policy re-layout. Target layout:

  w/{wId}/sandbox-egress-policy.json  workspace-wide policy (moved)
  w/{wId}/sandboxes/{ownerId}.json    owner policy; ownerId is a conversation
                                      sId or a pod space sId

Owner-keying makes the per-sandbox policy stable across sandbox
destroy/recreate cycles, lets pods reuse the same file slot with no third
storage location, and the w/{wId}/ prefix makes relocation and scrubbing a
prefix operation.

This proxy build reads BOTH layouts so it can deploy before front changes
anything:

- Optional ownerId JWT claim (back-compatible; sbId stays the required
  identity claim and remains in logs).
- Workspace lookup prefers w/{wId}/sandbox-egress-policy.json and falls back
  to the legacy workspaces/{wId}.json when absent (dated TODO to drop).
- Evaluation unions workspace + owner + legacy per-sandbox policies, all
  fail-closed, so in-flight approvals in legacy sandbox files keep working
  until those sandboxes age out (dated TODO to drop).
- /invalidate-policy accepts: wId (evicts both workspace layouts),
  wId + ownerId (owner entry), or sbId (legacy sandbox entry).

Inert until front mints ownerId and writes the new paths; this build must
deploy and be healthy before the front cutover.

[front] feat: db tools on the sandbox_functions server (list/schema/query/reconcile) (#28720)

* [front] feat: db tools on the sandbox_functions server (list/schema/query/reconcile)

With the stored schemas gone, agents get live database visibility from
conversations through four tools built on the call tool's boilerplate
(getPod/getWritablePodContext -> dsbx exec as agent-proxied with
DUST_POD_DATABASES_DIR pinned -> one-line JSON envelope):

- db_list: live {db}.db files with WAL-inclusive sizes (dsbx db list gets
  its front consumer back).
- db_schema: regenerate a drizzle schema file from the live SQLite file
  via the build_on_sandbox scratch-dir pattern (storage types only — the
  authored databases/{db}.db.ts stays the source of truth).
- db_query: one SQL statement, SELECT or DML, DDL refused by the runner;
  plain DML renders the affected-row count, spilled results keep the
  runner's note naming the sandbox file. Write-gated (it mutates data).
- db_reconcile: apply an edited schema file to the live database — the
  same additive-only gate as publish, serialized with publishes under the
  pod's publish lock.

The dsbx-level {error} envelope now maps per command: model-correctable

fix: upgrade Temporal TS SDK 1.15.0 → 1.15.1 (#28804)

Temporal published an advisory for a severe workflow-isolation bug in the
TypeScript SDK: with reuseV8Context: true (our default in both front and
connectors workers) and webpack >= 5.108.0, state can leak across workflow
executions (module-level vars, queries, stuck promises). Affected releases
include 1.15.0, which we pin exactly across connectors, front and
front/workers-build. The fix is 1.15.1.

We are not exposed today (resolved webpack < 5.108.0), but temporal's
unpinned transitive webpack range means a routine lockfile refresh could
flip both conditions true. Bumping the SDK removes the risk at the source.

- Bump @temporalio/{activity,client,common,worker,workflow,interceptors-opentelemetry}
  to 1.15.1 in connectors, front and front/workers-build.
- Regenerate lockfiles (front/connectors share the root workspaces lockfile;
  workers-build was also reconciled off its stale 1.12.1 pin).
- Temporarily lower .npmrc min-release-age 7 -> 1 so the 1.15.1 release
  (published 2026-07-08) is installable; TODO to rebump to 7 after 2026-07-15.

* feat(sandbox): scope pod conversations' egress policy to the Pod

Pod network settings apply to everything running in the Pod: conversation
sandboxes and the Pod's shared sandbox all read the same owner policy file,
keyed by the Pod space's sId — no per-conversation policy files inside Pods.

- The lifecycle ready helpers derive an egressPolicyOwnerId, distinct from

  and fail hard if GCS refuses, rather than best-effort after the fact — a
  stray file left behind is worse than an aborted delete the admin retries.
- egress_policy.ts: nest ownerId in the same object as policy on

fix(front): point offloaded tool-output snippets at the archived file (#28937)

Offloaded tool outputs are replaced in model context by an 8,000-char
snippet, but for resource-shaped blocks (webbrowser BROWSE_RESULT,
data-source DATA_SOURCE_NODE_CONTENT) the snippet dropped the pointer
to the offloaded file: the resource keeps the original URL as uri and
the scoped path was discarded. Agents could not read any browsed page
beyond 8,000 characters.

Offload snippets are now built by a shared makeOffloadedSnippet helper
that always appends '[Full content archived at {scopedPath}]' so the
model can read the full content back, and only emits the
'... (truncated)' marker when characters were actually dropped.

TaskDirectiveChipInner pattern (chip wrapped in a native button as the
popover trigger), which makes the link reachable by both mouse and

* [Admin Gov] Reshape group_permissions registry to role definitions

Express the registry as roles (named verb bundles valid at one or more levels) instead
of flat per-type verb lists. Valid verbs per (resourceType, level) are derived as the
union of the roles' verb sets, so the roles are the single source of truth.

Grants still store/validate a plain verb (the switch to storing the role name and
verb->role expansion at check time is a follow-up); this PR only changes the shape of
the registry and tightens validity to the intended role model:
- instance-level roles: space reader/member/admin, agent+skill editor.
- type-level capability roles are singletons: create/publish (agent+skill),
  invite/publish (frame), admin (billing+identity), read (audit_log), use (models_tier).
- drops currently-unused combos: instance publish on agent/skill, type-wide read/write
  on agent/skill, type-wide space grants.

Adds registry invariant tests: no two roles share a verb set, every verb is reachable,
every type-level role is a singleton.

* [Admin Gov] Store role names as group_permissions grant types

Grant types are now the registry-defined role names (space reader/member/admin, agent+skill
editor, and the singleton capabilities create/publish/invite/admin/read/use) rather than plain
verbs. Verbs become a separate vocabulary (GRANT_VERBS) used only to describe what a role grants.

- types: split GRANT_VERBS (capabilities) from GRANT_TYPES (stored role names).
- registry: assertValidGrant now checks the grant type is a role defined for the resource type at
  the required level, instead of deriving a verb set.
- no schema change and no live-writer change: the only stored grant types today are singletons
  (models_tier `use`; governance create/publish/invite/admin) whose role name equals the verb.

This is what makes revoke correct under additive multi-grant: overlapping roles (e.g. `member` and
`admin` on the same space) are distinct rows, so revoking one never destroys verbs held via the
other. Adds that revoke-collision regression test.

Verb->role expansion at check time is deferred: the only check today (hasWorkspacePermission) is
type-wide, where every role is a singleton, so no expansion is needed yet.

out of scope here.

every downstream variable/return is derived from the already-stripped

create unconditionally (Postgres' recommended recovery). Per external review.

feat(activation): ES-backed activation evaluator, wired into scheduler + CLI (#29123)

* feat(activation): ES-backed activation evaluator, wired into scheduler + CLI

Implements the "is a user activated" evaluator and gates the activation
nudge orchestration on it.

- evaluator.ts: batch evaluateActivation() runs ONE composite Elasticsearch
  aggregation per workspace over agent_message_analytics_2. A user is
  activated with >=6 organic high-value-use-case days spanning >=3 distinct
  Monday-based UTC weeks over a trailing 28d window. Programmatic origins are
  excluded in-query; nudge-caused conversations via excludedConversationIds
  (capped). Pure computeActivationFromCells is unit-tested.
- stake_and_frame_classification.ts: Tier-3 (Creation) is classified in TS
  from the day's distinct succeeded tools. Policy is stake-derived (internal
  tool stake != never_ask => write) plus a frame override for
  interactive_content; custom/remote tools never count. Tier-4 (orchestration
  / unsupervised) stays as static in-query filters.
- orchestrator.ts: determineEligibleActivationUsers considers pod editors,
  skips already-activated users, and runActivationForWorkspace emits one
  activation event per eligible (pod, user).
- trigger.ts: activation trigger filter + event now carry userId so a nudge
  only fires the target user's per-user pod trigger.
- Shared runActivationForWorkspace is used by both the activation_scheduler
  temporal activity and the admin CLI (identical logic).

Refs dust-tt/decisions#905

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* refactor(activation): simplify HVUC definition, extract ES query, harden batch

Follow-up to the initial evaluator, incorporating review:

- Simplify the "activated" definition: HVUC day = DAU day with >=1 succeeded
  advanced-cost tool call, frame touch (interactive_content), or run_agent.
  This is computed entirely in one in-query filter aggregation, removing the
  stake-derived TS classifier (stake_and_frame_classification.{ts,test.ts}

  unsupervised/triggered signal.

dsbx: never substitute DSEC secrets into CORS preflight headers

Access-Control-Request-Headers / Access-Control-Request-Method values are
routinely reflected by servers in Access-Control-Allow-Headers /
Access-Control-Allow-Methods responses. Substituting a placeholder there
round-trips the real secret back to the sandbox client, defeating the
placeholder model. Confirmed against play.google.com/log, which echoes the
requested header list verbatim.

Bump dsbx to 0.1.34 and dust-base image to 0.8.55

Ships the CORS preflight substitution fix. Bedrock stays at 1.10.0: the
dsbx install happens in the dust-base layer.

dsbx: extend DSEC substitution blocklist to remaining reflective headers

Follow-up to the CORS preflight fix. Audit of the standard request header
list against is_unsafe_substitution_header found more headers whose values
come back to the client by design or by convention:

- sec-websocket-protocol / sec-websocket-extensions: echoed in the 101
  handshake response (the dsbx upgrade path still substitutes headers
  before splicing raw frames).
- idempotency-key: echoed by APIs in 409/422 error bodies.
- content-disposition: filenames echoed in upload responses and errors.
- prefer: RFC 7240 Preference-Applied can mirror the value.
- expect: a 417 response can quote the failed expectation.
- last-event-id: occasionally reflected by SSE endpoints.

Bumps dsbx to 0.1.35 and dust-base image to 0.8.56 to ship it.

[front] Only the conversation creator can add Spaces to an existing conversation

Selected Spaces are a conjunctive access requirement: a viewer needs read access to
every Space in `conversation.requestedSpaceIds` to read the conversation. There is no
removal path today, so appending a Space is irreversible.

The append endpoint only gated on the caller being able to read the conversation, so
any reader of a shared conversation could permanently evict every other participant
(including themselves and their own messages) by selecting a Space the others lack.

`addSelectedConversationSpaces` now takes an explicit `enforceCreatorOnly` flag,
implemented with the existing `ConversationResource.isConversationCreator` helper:
- true on the two paths where a user widens an existing conversation (the
  selected_spaces append endpoint and posting a message with selectedSpaceIds),
- false on conversation creation (the conversation is brand new and has no
  participant row yet, participation is upserted afterwards) and on run_agent
  sub-agent inheritance (system-initiated, and the Spaces were already revalidated
  against the same user on the parent).

The new `conversation_not_creator` domain code maps to HTTP 403.

[front] Only gate the creator check on an actual widening of the conversation ACL

The input bar resends the conversation's whole current selection in
`context.selectedSpaceIds` on every message, so gating every non-empty call
locked non-creator participants out of posting in any conversation that already
had selected Spaces. Re-selecting a Space the conversation already requires
cannot evict anyone, so only run the creator check when the request adds a Space
that is not already in `conversation.requestedSpaceIds`.

Do not honour selected Spaces in pod conversations

Selecting a Space from the input bar does two things: it appends the Space
to the conversation requestedSpaceIds (a conjunctive ACL requirement) and it
widens the agent runtime scope for that conversation. The ACL narrowing is
the only thing that makes the widened scope safe.

Pod conversations pin their ACL to the project space by design, so they
cannot carry that extra requirement. Selection is blocked at every write
path for them, but the runtime path was not, and nothing cleaned up the
selection rows when a conversation moved into a project. The result:

1. Alice selects the restricted "Legal" Space in a normal conversation. The
   ACL and the selection row both include Legal.
2. Alice moves the conversation into a team project.
   moveConversationToProject overwrites requestedSpaceIds with the project
   space, dropping Legal. The selection row survives.
3. The conversation is now readable by every project member, Legal access or
   not.
4. Alice posts. getValidSelectedSpaceIdsForAgentRun still returns Legal, so
   the agent retrieves Legal documents into the conversation.
5. Everyone in the project reads them. The picker is hidden in pod
   conversations, so nothing signals that Spaces are still attached.

Two fixes, both needed:

- getValidSelectedSpaceIdsForAgentRun now returns [] for pod conversations,
  mirroring what updateConversationRequirementsForSkills already does.
- moveConversationToProject soft-removes the conversation selections inside
  the transaction that resets the requirements.

The guard alone is not enough: moving the conversation back out of the
project calls rebuildConversationRequirements, which rebuilds
requestedSpaceIds from agents and content fragments only. The conversation
stops being a pod conversation, the guard stops applying, and the stale
selections go live again with no ACL backing.

Clear selected Spaces when a conversation moves out of a project

Clearing selections on move-in only covers conversations moved in from now
on. Conversations already sitting in a project with active selection rows
still exist, and Part A only keeps those rows inert while the conversation
is a pod. On the way out, rebuildConversationRequirements rebuilds
requestedSpaceIds from agents and content fragments only, so the selection
becomes live again with no ACL backing.

Clear selections in moveConversationOutOfProject as well, before dropping
the project association so no intermediate state has a live selection
outside a project. Idempotent single UPDATE, so no backfill needed.

Also drop the move-in test duplicated from selected_spaces.test.ts and note
that removeForConversation is retained for the future deselect path.

Drop duplicated move-in test, document removeForConversation

The move-in clearing test in projects/conversations.test.ts asserted exactly
what selected_spaces.test.ts already covers, at the cost of re-inlining the
space/group/membership setup. Keep the one next to the feature.

Point the pod-conversation test at the memberProjectSpace helper, and note
on removeForConversation that it is the deselect-path counterpart of
upsertForConversation rather than dead code.

Fix lost update on conversation requestedSpaceIds

Attaching a Space from the input bar does two things: it appends the Space to
conversation.requestedSpaceIds (a conjunctive ACL — a viewer needs read access
to every listed Space) and it widens the agent runtime scope for that
conversation, which is what reaches real knowledge retrieval. The ACL narrowing
is the only thing that makes the scope widening safe.

The merge was computed from the caller's conversation snapshot and then written
with updateRequirements, which overwrites the column. The picker fires one POST
per checkbox toggle with no in-flight serialization and the dropdown stays open
on select, so ticking several Spaces quickly produces overlapping requests. Under
READ COMMITTED they interleave:

  req 1: snapshot [A] -> writes [A, X]
  req 2: snapshot [A] -> writes [A, Y]

Final ACL is [A, Y] while both selection rows committed and are active. X is in
the agent's scope with no ACL requirement backing it, so users without access to
X can read a conversation containing X's data.

Add ConversationResource.appendRequestedSpaceIds, which re-reads the conversation
row with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE inside the caller's transaction, unions the locked
value with the new ids and writes the result. Concurrent appends now serialize on
the row, and the selection rows and the ACL can no longer disagree.
addSelectedConversationSpaces uses it instead of the snapshot-based computation,
and returns the persisted ACL as effectiveAcl.spaceIds — the message-post and
conversation-create endpoints feed that value back into their local conversation
object, so it has to be the real post-merge value rather than an optimistic local
union.

Also pass the transaction through to fetchById in the existing static
updateRequirements (and thread it through the conversation fetch path) so that
read participates in the enclosing transaction instead of running on another
connection.

Pass sandbox function error codes through instead of re-deriving them

Follow-up on #28968. The Frame parent turned every API error but one into
`invocation_failed`, so a 403, a 400 and a 500 all reached Frame code as the
same code and the endpoint's own classification was lost. Forward the API
error type instead, and drop the viz-side copy of the code list so a code viz
has not heard of yet survives rather than becoming `transport_error`.

Also close the two gaps that made a failed call hard to trace at all:
`fail()` persisted only the message, so `inspect_invocations` could never show
the code, and nothing logged the failure on the way out to the iframe.

Frames get the error by rejection now, and React error boundaries do not catch
async rejections, so a Frame awaiting `callFunction` without a `catch` renders
nothing and reports nothing. Route unhandled rejections into the existing
error path.

Address review feedback

- Drop the stale `function_not_found` from the private swagger enum, and drop
  the enum itself since the code is open by design. Regenerated swagger.json.
- Degrade instead of throwing on an unreadable invocation blob. Listings load
  every invocation's blob, so one bad record (including one written by a newer
  deploy mid-rollout) was failing the whole listing.
- Pipe the legacy error arm back through the object schema so both arms infer
  one shape and `status` is readable without narrowing. Export the type, it
  appears in the exported `SandboxFunctionInvocationForLLM`.
- Log `fileId` rather than a second name for the same value, and add
  workspaceId/conversationId.
- Seed the legacy blob test through the bucket like the neighbouring test, with
  a message the current code never writes so it can actually fail.

Version the invocation blob instead of sniffing its shape

The version field existed but was never bumped, so blobs carrying the new
error shape still claimed version 1 and the reader had to guess from the shape.
Bump to 2 and discriminate on it: each shape we have written is an arm, a new
one is an added arm rather than a wider guess, and v1 migrates on read.

Also drop the gcsPath parameter. It was only there to carry a class member into
a log line, so do the logging in loadDataFromGcs which already has it. The
parse helper now covers malformed JSON too, which was still throwing and would
have taken down a listing the same way an unreadable blob did.

Rebase over the invocation context field, tighten the migration

The branch was behind #29392, which added `context` to this same schema. Rebased
and resolved it, then hardened the two spots that made it easy to drop:

- Derive the current-version type from the v2 arm with Extract instead of
  hand-writing it, so the two cannot disagree. Adding `context` to the schema
  no longer needs a matching edit somewhere else.
- Spread in the v1 migration rather than listing fields. Listing them compiled
  fine while silently dropping `context` from every v1 blob on read, and
  permanently on the next write.

Reuse the existing safeParseJSON helper, and settle on one name for the stored
error rather than three.

[DX] stop the sparkle watcher from deleting dist when mprocs stops (#29542)

Stopping mprocs left sparkle/dist deleted, so `tsgo` in front (and any other
consumer) failed with "Cannot find module '@dust-tt/sparkle'" until sparkle was
rebuilt by hand.

sparkle's watch is npm-watch, i.e. nodemon, and nodemon binds SIGHUP to
`restart` whenever its `signal` option is SIGUSR2 (the default) -- see
lib/nodemon.js:161. Tearing down the proc's terminal delivers exactly that
SIGHUP, so nodemon started a fresh `npm run build`, whose first step is
`rm -rf dist`, and was killed about a second later. Deleting dist takes ~1s;
rebuilding it takes ~7s, so dist stayed deleted.

Setting `signal` to any non-SIGUSR2 value leaves SIGHUP unbound, so nodemon
terminates on shutdown instead of starting a build. SIGTERM is not a valid
choice here: run.js:239 restarts whenever the child exits via `config.signal`,
which reintroduces the wipe through the shutdown SIGTERM. SIGQUIT behaves like
SIGUSR2 (catchable, terminates by default) without being a signal the shutdown
path delivers.

Also drop the `trap 'npm run build; exit' TERM INT` line added in #29464. mprocs
runs each proc as `/bin/sh -c <script>`, and because the script is
newline-separated with a simple last command, /bin/sh exec()s `npm run watch`
over itself and the trap is discarded -- so it never ran on macOS. Its intent
(a current sparkle build after stopping) holds anyway: the watcher rebuilds on
every src change, so dist is already up to date when the watcher exits.

Extends the activation scheduler workflow to enumerate and gate every
pod once per day, then visit each eligible pod at a deterministic slot
spread across the regional workday window instead of nudging them all
at once. Re-gates each pod right before sending, since state can go

adds an on-demand signalWithStart trigger for poke/admin-forced cycles
through the same code path.

Prioritize awake sandboxes in the sandbox reaper, sleep idle ones faster

Image rollouts kill-request the whole fleet (tens of thousands of
sandboxes, mostly sleeping), and the kill sweep starved the pause sweep,
so idle running sandboxes piled up and inflated E2B cluster concurrency.

- Split kill_requested into two phases: awake sandboxes (running /
  pending_approval) first, sleeping ones last, most recently active
  first since those are the likeliest to be woken by a returning user.
  Sleeping kills are optional cleanup: ensureActive already destroys and
  recreates kill-requested sandboxes on access.
- Reorder phases so pausing stale running sandboxes runs before kills.
- Double MAX_BATCHES_PER_PHASE to 200; the 100-batch cap was the
  bottleneck when draining rollout backlogs.
- Lower the default sleep threshold from 10 to 5 minutes to cut the
  idle tail of each sandbox session.
- Add a partial index on (lastActivityAt, id) for kill-requested
  sleeping sandboxes to back the new sweep.
Address review: factory opt for lastActivityAt, comment on compat activity
Document why the sleeping kill sweep goes most recently active first
Document post-deploy drain to drop reaper phase patch immediately.
Reorder reaper phases: kill awake first, then sleep, then sleeping kills.

threw and the error boundary replaced the whole page, so a Frame needing a
personal connection just failed instead of prompting.

Pass the viewer (workspace + user) as props instead: the app path derives it
from `AuthContext`, the shared Frame from `useUser()` and the workspace the
viewer is a member of.

Also fix a second card appearing after authenticating. A Frame can have several
invocations in flight, each blocked on the same connection, and each rendered
its own card; resolving one left the others blocked until their sandbox token
expired. The blocked-action queue now lives in the iframe, which sees every
invocation, so one card resolves the whole group.

by clicking a slug in the pod's Pod Functions table. It shows the function's

of the workspace they inspect, so "viewer" resolves no user and returns nothing.
Kept distinct from "system", which is reserved for paths that already validated

perf: index spaces by id in baseFetchWithAuthorization (#30004)

Resolving each blob's space with a linear scan over `spaces` costs
O(blobs x spaces), and both sides of the comparison go through Sequelize
attribute getters, which allocate on every read. On large fetches that
dominates allocation and keeps the event loop busy for the whole loop.

fix: batch file deletion on workspace hard delete (#30005)

* fix: batch file deletion on workspace hard delete

Deleting every file of a workspace in a single statement exceeds the
Postgres statement timeout on large workspaces. Each attempt runs for
300s, writes gigabytes of WAL, then rolls back, so the activity retries
forever without making progress while the whole front DB pays for it.

Delete in batches of 10k instead, so each statement stays short and the
deletion moves forward across retries.

Fix Academy quiz greeting displaying the raw text "{contentType}" (#29973)

Before this change, the Dust Academy quiz greeted visitors with the literal
characters "{contentType}" on screen:

    "Ready to test your understanding of this {contentType}?"

instead of naming the kind of content being quizzed. This was visible on
every Academy quiz — courses, chapters and lessons alike.

The greeting text comes from the Contentful "quizSettings" entry, whose
English copy uses a {contentType} placeholder. AcademyQuiz substituted the
other placeholders it knows about ({name} in the greeting, {passing} and
{total} in the fail message) but never substituted {contentType}, so that
one was rendered verbatim. Every caller was already passing the value in;
the component just never used it for the greeting.

The greeting now reads "Ready to test your understanding of this course?"
(or "lesson", or "chapter"), using the contentType prop that all three
Academy quiz pages already supply.

No other text changes. The French copy spells the word out rather than
using the placeholder, and the built-in fallback copy has no placeholder
either; substituting an absent placeholder leaves those strings untouched.

Return Pod function results in the invocation response when they settle in time

The invocation endpoint returns as soon as the workflow is launched, so a Frame calling a Pod
function pays a second round trip to the event stream for a result that was usually ready in
under a second.

Behind sandbox_function_fast_execution, the endpoint waits a short while for the invocation to
settle and returns its outcome inline.

The wait stops as soon as the invocation blocks on a tool approval or on personal
authentication. Holding the response there would deadlock: the approval card only renders once
the client holds the invocation and subscribes to its stream. Clients that get no outcome
subscribe as before, and the stream replays from history everything already published.

A Pod function that calls tools may wait on the user for approval or authentication, for as long

[front] Warn about broken Pod function callers before restricting a Pod (#30050)

* [front] Warn about broken Pod function callers before restricting a Pod

Restricting a Pod drops the workspace global group, so anyone who is neither a Pod
member nor a workspace admin loses read access to its space and can no longer invoke
its functions -- silently breaking any Frame they were driving.

Adds a pre-flight estimate on the visibility toggle: how many recent invocations came
from users who would lose access, and how many such users there are.

No schema change -- `sandbox_function_invocations` already records `userId` and
`createdAt`.

* Skip the access lookups on the counts, not the function list

The `sandboxFunctions.length === 0` early return bought nothing for correctness -- the
normal path already produced identical zeros -- and its only real value, skipping the
member and admin lookups, was gated on the narrower of the two empty cases: a Pod whose
functions saw no traffic in the window still paid for both queries.

Guard on the counts instead, and pull the lookups into a helper so there is one return
statement and one zero shape.

Run fast Pod function invocations without the invocation workflow

A fast function only reads and writes pod state, so its invocation has nothing to survive: it
cannot block on a tool approval, and it settles in well under a second. Routing it through a
Temporal workflow costs a workflow start and an activity dispatch for durability it never uses.

Behind sandbox_function_fast_execution, a fast invocation executes in the request that creates
it. The workflow still owns durable functions, and fast invocations whose sandbox is not already
running.

execute() gains an inline mode for that, which constrains it twice.

The sandbox is used only if it is already running, never created, woken or recreated, which
ensureActive enforces under the lifecycle lock. A caller-side status check is not enough: a
kill-requested sandbox reports itself as running until it is destroyed and recreated, and every
image rollout marks running sandboxes, so a cold start could still land inside the request.

Execution is bounded at 10s instead of the workflow's 2 minutes. Past that the invocation is
failed rather than retried durably, since it may already have written to pod state.

An inline invocation that fails records its own outcome, as the workflow's activity does, so
listeners settle instead of waiting for a workflow that never ran.

Deny tool calls to Pod functions published as fast

A fast function is published on the promise that it does not call tools, and fast execution
depends on that promise: a tool call can block on approval or authentication for as long as the
user takes, which an invocation running inside a request cannot survive. Nothing enforced it, so
a mislabelled function would hold a request for as long as the tool call polls.

Mint the invocation token without tool access for a fast function, and refuse the tool-call
endpoint when it is presented. The mode decides this, not the transport, so a fast function
behaves the same whether it ran inline or through the workflow.

noTools is required rather than defaulted, since a minting site that forgets it would silently
grant tool access. The claim has to be declared on the token payload schema to survive
verification, which strips what it does not know.

Fix: bogus tooltip for default agent

Record a Pod function as durable when it calls a Dust tool as fast

A fast function is published on the promise that it does not call Dust tools, and the refusal that
enforces it is also the only evidence the promise was wrong. Today that evidence goes nowhere: the
invocation fails, and the next one fails identically, because the declaration that caused it is
still on the function.

Record the function as durable from the refusal path. The invocation that triggered it still
fails, since the tool call was already refused, but every later one runs durably and works. The
publisher does not have to notice anything for a mislabelled function to start behaving.

The write is guarded on the mode still being fast, so concurrent invocations that each break the
promise converge on one write and a function whose publisher already moved it is left alone. It is
never awaited by the request: the refusal is already decided, and a slow write must not delay it.

Since a publish restates the mode, this is an override the publisher clears rather than a
permanent verdict. A republished bundle that still calls tools is simply recorded again.

Also logs inline execution failures. The other case worth healing is a fast function that runs past
its ceiling, but a timeout arrives as an ordinary provider failure with nothing marking it as one,
and one slow run is much weaker evidence than a refused tool call. Log the class first and decide
with numbers.

[front] fix: filter high stake tools on activation origin (#30116)

Tell agents how to choose a Pod function execution mode, and make them choose

The mode is the publisher's call and it shapes how functions are split up, rather than being a
flag set at the end. The publish tool now requires it: a mode the model has to state on every
publish is a decision it has to make, and it removes the trap where omitting the field on a
re-publish quietly moved a fast function back to durable.

The skill explains the split that matters for a Frame. A path the Frame polls should be fast and
serve Pod state; when it needs data from an external system, the fix is not to make that path
durable but to split it, with a durable function writing what the tool returns into a database and
a fast function serving that database. A read that must be live on every call is simply durable
and slower.

It also spells out what fast forbids, which is narrower than it sounds: only `dsbx tools`. Pod

[front] perf: run sandbox commands in a single round trip

Every sandbox operation paid Sandbox.connect before it could address the
sandbox, and every command carrying stdin paid two more calls to send and
close it. A fast Pod function therefore made four sequential round trips to
E2B before its output could stream back.

Cache the connected handle per provider id for 5 minutes, and pass stdin that
fits through the environment so the command wrapper can pipe it in. That
leaves one round trip.

Measured against a real dust-base sandbox: a cached connection with inline
stdin runs in the same time as one with no stdin at all, while the streamed
stdin path costs about 350ms more, which is the two extra round trips.

fixup: keep envd owning the workload pid, and make inline stdin opt-in

Two problems found by review and confirmed against a live sandbox.

The pipeline wrapper broke timeout enforcement. envd signals only the pid it
started, so piping into the command left it holding the wrapper shell while
the workload ran on as a grandchild: a timed-out command kept running in the
sandbox after we gave up on it. Measured, a command with inline stdin was
still ticking 4s after its deadline while the same command without stdin had
stopped. The wrapper now execs the command through a process substitution, so
the pid envd owns is the pid that matters, and all paths stop on timeout.

Inline stdin is now opt-in per call. Commands.list reports the environment of
every running command, and the four root call sites that pass stdin are
handing over egress secrets, the egress token, a GCS token and the env
manifest, each with a comment saying stdin is used precisely to keep those out
of process metadata. Those keep the streamed path. Only the Pod function
invocation opts in, where the payload is the function's own input and the exec
already carries a token in its environment.

fixup: evict only the connection entry the failing call used

With a batch of calls failing together on one stale handle, an unscoped drop
let each straggler evict the good handle that the first one had already
reconnected, so every call in the batch paid its own connect.

[front] perf: trim the fast Pod function invocation setup path

Four independent costs paid serially on every fast invocation:

The initial GCS blob write and the created-event publish sat between row
creation and execution, though nothing before the terminal transition reads
either. On the inline path both now run concurrently with execution, and
succeed()/fail() await them before the terminal blob write and result
publish, which keeps the blob write ordered and the created event ahead of
the result event. The durable path still awaits both before the workflow
starts, since the workflow reads the blob.

execute() re-fetched the function, authorized, and readied the sandbox one
after the other; the function check chain and the sandbox readiness chain
are independent and now overlap.

execute() wrote lastActivityAt a second time right after ensureActive wrote
it under the lifecycle lock; the duplicate is gone, and the write itself is
now throttled to 30s granularity, since the reaper compares it against
minutes-scale inactivity thresholds and every invocation was hammering the
shared sandbox row.

Both invocation callers subscribed to the Redis event stream to read back
an outcome the inline execution had already produced in this process. The
terminal transitions now record the outcome on the instance, and callers
short-circuit on it, falling back to the stream only for invocations that
escalated to the workflow.

fixup: guard the deferral's cross-process readers

Review found the deferred initial blob write unsafe for the two consumers
that read the blob from another process. The workflow-escalation path now
settles the pending persistence and re-runs the blob write synchronously
before launching, failing the request if it cannot land, so the activity
(one attempt, ~600ms of read retries) always finds the blob and a failed
deferred write can no longer strand a terminal row without one. And the
deferral now requires stdout delivery as well as inline execution: with
callback delivery dsbx POSTs to a route that fetches the invocation blob
mid-execution, inside the deferral window.

The preflight overlap is now inline-only: on the durable path sandbox
readiness may create or wake a sandbox, a paid side effect that stays
gated behind the function and authorization checks.

Also from review: a rejected created-event publish is logged instead of
silently swallowed by allSettled, the activity-write throttle gets a unit
test, and the reaper config notes the 30s floor the throttle imposes on
SANDBOX_SLEEP_THRESHOLD_MS overrides.
fixup: exhaustive switch on the settled outcome

dsbx: pin Host to the approved domain on port 80

The plain-HTTP guard extracted the domain from the first request's Host,
handed it to the proxy for approval, then forwarded every later request on
the keep-alive connection without checking its Host again. The proxy only
splices bytes after the handshake, so a connection opened to an allowlisted
CDN-fronted domain could front any other host on that CDN, in both
directions, with nothing in the deny log.

normalized_authority now pins the per-request authority to the domain
approved for the connection in both modes, SNI on 443 and the first
request's Host on 80, instead of TLS only. Mismatches deny with the new
host_domain_mismatch reason and tear the connection down.

Side effect of pinning the full authority: a Host carrying a non-default
port on a port-80 connection now denies, matching what 443 already did.
That guard only runs when the original destination was really port 80, so
such a Host misstates the authority the proxy connected to.

Log harness deny reasons and cover the self-consistent proxy-form request

Review follow-ups.

Harness deny reasons (host_domain_mismatch, host_sni_mismatch, ...) were
dropped before reaching the agent and never logged anywhere else, so a
request-policy denial was invisible in production. That is a bad place to
be right after tightening one of those checks: we could not tell a real
fronting attempt from legitimate traffic we just broke. Split the filter
into agent-facing lines and harness denials and log the latter.

The absolute-URI test did not gate the pin: the existing check compares the
target against the request's own Host, so the mismatched pair already
denied before this change. Added the self-consistent pair, which used to
pass both checks on port 80.

Also noted that the pin ends at a WebSocket 101, where we splice frames
unparsed.

[front] Namespace published pod functions by app folder (#30178)

* [front] Namespace published pod functions by app folder

A published pod function was identified by a slug unique per pod, so two apps in
the same pod could not both own a function called `refresh`: the second publish
silently replaced the first, bundle and contract included.

The published slug becomes `<app>__<name>`, where publish derives the prefix from
the app folder the source lives in. Only that folder contributes, so `functions/`
and anything nested under it never appear in the slug, and moving a source inside
its app does not rename the function.

Encoding the prefix in the slug rather than nesting directories keeps the rest of
the chain untouched: `__` already passes dsbx's is_valid_name and resolves in the
flat read_dir of $DUST_FUNCTIONS_DIR, and `podId/slug` stays a two-segment
reference. No migration, no CLI change, no route change. Bare slugs stay valid so
functions published before this, and the Frames referencing them, keep working.

Publishing from the pod root is now rejected: without an app folder there is no
prefix to derive, and the skill already required one.

* [viz] Accept app-prefixed slugs in the Frame's function reference grammar

The viz workspace carries its own copy of the slug grammar, because it cannot
import from front. Namespacing published slugs widened front's copy but not this
one, so `usePodFunction("<podId>/tasklist__add-task")` failed validation, resolved
to a null SWR key, and the Frame issued no request at all — a broken function with
nothing in the network tab.

Move the reference grammar to its own module so front can import it, and assert
from front that the two accept exactly the same slugs. Same arrangement as the
runner protocol in cli/dust-sandbox/functions-runner/protocol.ts.

* [front] Allow pod functions published from the pod root

Publish rejected a source sitting directly at the pod root, on the grounds that
without an app folder there is no prefix to derive and the namespace guarantee
would be advisory only.

That was enforcement in the wrong layer. The guarantee that matters, that two apps
cannot clobber each other, holds regardless: a root function is not in an app, and
the namespaces are disjoint by construction. A name is a single slug segment so it
carries no `__`, and a normalized prefix carries none either, so every prefixed
slug has exactly one and every bare slug has none. What remains is that two root
functions can clobber each other, the same tradeoff already accepted for two
functions inside one app.

A root source now publishes under its bare name. The skill still says to use an
app folder, and now says why: moving a source into one later renames its function,
leaving the old slug published and stale.

* [front] Attribute the qualified reference to Frames in publish's output

The message said "Call it by reference <podId>/<slug>", but the call tool takes
the slug alone: it resolves the pod from the run context. Only a Frame needs the
qualified reference, so name that consumer instead of implying the MCP tools want
it.

[front] fix sandbox function staging reads against symlink swap (TOCTOU)

buildSandboxFunctionOnSandbox and getDatabaseSchemaOnSandbox stage artifacts
in agent-writable /tmp dirs as agent-proxied, then read them back through the
provider file API, which envd serves as root while following symlinks. Code
running as the agent on the same sandbox VM could swap a staging file for a
symlink to a root-only file (e.g. /run/dust/egress-secrets.json) between the
exec and the read, and the root read would return that file's content to the
caller or persist it as a published function bundle.

Pin each artifact to the sha256 captured at the end of the producing exec and
fail closed on mismatch. A swap before the capture fails the capture itself
(set -e: sha256sum cannot open the swapped target as agent-proxied); a swap
after the capture no longer hashes equal. Error messages never carry content,
so a swapped-in file cannot leak through the error path either.

[front] staging integrity: full-line marker split, stderr hint on missing hash

Review feedback: anchor the stdout split on the last full-line marker so a
model printing the marker string cannot shadow the real capture or truncate
its own output mid-stream, and include the exec stderr in the missing-hash
error so a failed capture (e.g. sha256sum denied on a swapped target) is
debuggable.

[front] staging integrity: split stdout only on staging execs

Splitting every dsbx db command's stdout at the capture marker let code the
command imports (the model-written schema file during reconcile) print a
forged envelope followed by a marker line and shadow the real envelope,
which is otherwise always the last stdout line. Gate the split on an
explicit stagingCapture flag that only db schema sets.

[sparkle] Fix ContentMessage staying light in dark mode (#30250)

The Figma redesign (#30172) replaced the semantic color tokens with raw
palette classes (`bg-stone-50`, `text-red-800`, `bg-orange-50`, ...). Only
the semantic scales are remapped in the `.dark` block of `tokens.css` — raw
palette steps hold the same absolute value in both themes — so every variant
built on them rendered near-white on the dark canvas. `primary` was the most
visible: the blocked-actions banner above the input bar and the tool
validation card both use it.

Declare the dark side explicitly from the Figma spec, the way `Chip.tsx` does,
one palette family per variant with a fixed role per step: background 950,
stroke 900, text and icon 100. The neutral runs its own steps (950/800/50) — a
colored stroke reads on a colored fill, but on the near-black neutral surface
it has to stay quiet.

Leaning on the semantic scales instead would not match: their `.dark` remap
lands on different steps, and the orange ramp is not hue-stable (73.7deg at
step 50, 36.3deg at 950, the same hue as red-950), so `info`/`golden` came out
red rather than amber.

Light is untouched: all nine variants render byte-identical to `main` on
background, border and text. In dark, every background and text color matches
the spec exactly; the `highlight`/`blue` stroke is 8 RGB units off because the
`Blue/900` Figma variable and our `blue-900` token have drifted apart. Using
the token rather than hardcoding the hex.

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

[dsbx] chore: script to push @dust/pod into a running sandbox (#30262)

@dust/pod is vendored into the sandbox image at build time and published
function bundles keep it as an external import, so neither rebuilding dsbx nor
republishing a function picks up a change to it -- only a new image does. That
makes iterating on the package needlessly slow, and the reason is not written
down anywhere.

Add upsert_pod_package_to_sandbox.sh, mirroring upsert_dsbx_to_sandbox.sh (same
flags, same fzf picker, same e2b base64 push), and document why the package is
invisible to the other two rebuild paths.

Two details worth knowing:

- The build uses the same bun flags as buildPodPackage, so what lands is
  byte-identical to what a rebuilt image would ship, and it is written 644
  root:root like the image's own copy.
- The push is followed by dropping the warm function servers. A resident server
  holds the module it imported at startup, so replacing the file on disk alone
  changes nothing for it and the push looks successful while doing nothing.

[dsbx] feat: per-invocation context for pod runtime env

The function runner can now execute an invocation inside an
AsyncLocalStorage context carrying that invocation's environment, and
@dust/pod (currentUser, db, new podEnv) reads the environment through the
context instead of process.env. The storage is shared between the runner
bundle and the vendored package through the Symbol.for registry, since the
two are distinct module graphs.

Inside a context only the context env is consulted, so one invocation's
environment can never leak into another; outside any context (cold runs,
local use) reads fall back to process.env unchanged. invoke() takes the
per-invocation env as an optional argument; the v1 warm server still swaps
process.env, so behavior is unchanged until the concurrent server lands on
top of this.

* fix: don't create WorkOS users on dsync deprovisioning paths

The dsync group.user_removed, user.deleted and user.updated(inactive)
handlers all resolved the WorkOS user through
fetchOrCreateWorkOSUserWithEmail. When the directory user's email had no
WorkOS User Management user, that helper created one and added it to the
organization, then the local lookup by the freshly minted workOSUserId
could never match, so the activity threw and Temporal retried forever.

Add a fetch-only fetchWorkOSUserWithEmail and use it on the three
deprovisioning paths, treating a missing user as a no-op like
handleGroupDelete already does. Deprovisioning something that isn't
there is success, not failure.

A user that exists in WorkOS but has no local row means provisioning never
went through, which is worth surfacing rather than silently skipping. Keep

[front] fix: bound the kill-requested pre-destroy flush retry

A kill-requested sandbox whose pre-destroy flush can never succeed was
retried forever: the reaper re-ran the check every sweep, logged a panic,
and skipped the destroy, pinning a running VM and holding up the image
rollout indefinitely.

Give the flush a one hour grace period. Within it the behaviour is
unchanged (skip and retry next sweep, so transient GCS or daemon hiccups
still resolve). Past it the destroy proceeds despite the failing flush,
matching what dangerouslyDestroyAndRecreate already does, and logs that
unreplicated pod state is being dropped.

fix(dsbx): create function-authored files group-writable

The pod-state directories are setgid with a g::rwx default ACL, but a
default ACL only masks the mode a process asks for — it cannot restore
bits the umask stripped. With the inherited umask, a SQLite database a
function opens directly landed at 0640 owned agent-proxied:agent, so
litestream (dust-state, group agent) could read it but never write it,
and every replication sync failed with SQLITE_READONLY forever.

Set umask 007 in the runner so everything a function creates keeps the
group-writable guarantee that dsbx db reconcile already chmods in by
hand. Other stays empty: group agent is the sandbox's own trust boundary.

Bumps dsbx to 0.1.45 and dust-base to 0.8.70.

[dsbx] feat: concurrent warm function server with bounded admission

The per-function warm server (protocol v2) now runs invocations
concurrently: IO-bound calls interleave on the event loop like a web
server's, so overlapping invocations of one function no longer fan out
into cold runs (18% of runs in a real multi-user session). Per-invocation
state rides the invocation context from the previous commit instead of a
process.env swap, which is what makes concurrency safe.

Admission is bounded: 32 invocations in flight, then a FIFO queue of up
to 128 waiting at most 2s, then a structured overloaded outcome. The
refusal is deliberately not a cold fallback: unbounded cold runs under
saturation are what would exhaust the sandbox's memory.

The ack-before-execute contract is unchanged, and is why this stays a raw
line protocol rather than moving behind an HTTP server: the ack is a
synchronous socket write whose failure proves the client is gone, so a
client abandoning a queued request can never race into a duplicate
execution. Staleness (stat + stamped bundle hash) now drains the server
(stop listening, refuse the queue, finish in-flight work, exit) instead of
killing it mid-flight, and the same drain handles the lifetime cap, an RSS
recycle threshold, and hung invocations.

review: O(1) live-queue accounting with compaction, front overloaded code, drop orphaned fixture

The settled-entry queue could grow unbounded (and cost an O(n) scan per
request) while every slot stayed busy with long invocations: track the
live count directly, compact the array when settled entries dominate, and
key admission/idle/drain decisions off the live count. Front learns the
overloaded runner code so a refusal surfaces as itself instead of an
invalid-envelope invocation_failed. slow.ts lost its only consumer to the
concurrency rewrite. Also document the accepted residual race at the
first-frame timeout boundary.

review: close the ack races and scope the write-path state

A partial ack write now aborts like a failed one (the client would read a
truncated frame, classify the connection dead pre-ack and go cold, so
executing would risk the duplicate the ack exists to prevent), and a
request older than 3s is refused instead of acked: the client abandons at
4s, and acking into its walk-away window was the one remaining
double-execution race. Also moves the pending-write map into serve()'s
scope with the rest of the server state.

rework: pod-scoped generic worker pool with app affinity

Per-function servers bound memory by function count, which has no ceiling:
a pod with dozens of hot functions would out-eat the sandbox. Replace them
with a pool of 4 generic workers behind slot sockets. The request names
the function; the worker resolves and imports the bundle lazily and caches
it, so warm memory is bounded by the pool regardless of how many functions
the pod publishes.

Routing hashes the app prefix of the slug (app folders publish as
app__function), so all of one app's functions share a home worker: opening
an app pays one process spawn ever, and its working set (shared lib
imports included) accumulates in one module cache. Root-level slugs hash
as themselves. The client talks only to the home slot; the cold path
spawns the home worker.

Concurrency, admission, the ack contract and drain semantics are
unchanged from the previous commit. Warm timings gain an additive
importKind (cached|fresh) to observe affinity effectiveness.

[dsbx] perf: content-addressed bundle cache, hash-addressed warm imports

Cold runs: a stamped invocation whose bundle sits in the local cache
(~/.dust-fn/bundles/<sha256>.js) runs from the cached copy, skipping the
gcsfuse readdir and read entirely. Population happens after a resolved
cold run and re-hashes the bytes it just read, so gcsfuse serving stale
bytes cannot pin the stale version under the new hash. Entries unused for
7 days are pruned opportunistically.

Warm workers: a stamped republish now imports the new version from the
cache path instead of draining. The module cache is keyed by path, so the
new bytes load alongside the old module and every other bundle keeps its
warmth; the abandoned module lingers until the routine RSS recycle. A
stamped mismatch with no cache entry refuses without draining (the cold
run populates the cache; the next warm request imports it). Only
unstamped legacy staleness still recycles the worker.

The cache key is the publish-time hash front stamps on every invocation,
so serving stale is impossible by construction, and the fuse mount's
deliberate no-cache config stays untouched.

[front] enh: namespace pod databases by app (#30263)

* [front] enh: namespace pod databases by app

A pod's databases were a single flat namespace: two apps in one pod could not
both own a `chat` without colliding, and the pod_functions skill had to tell the
model to pick a name that would not clash with another app's.

Namespace them by app, the same way published function slugs already are. The
app prefix is never written in the function's source -- it is derived from where
the code lives (the schema file's app folder when reconciling, the function's
slug when invoking) and reaches the runtime as DUST_POD_DATABASE_PREFIX. That is
what makes an app folder copyable inside a pod: the copy publishes under its own
prefix and gets its own databases with no source edit.

Prefixing the FILE name (`myapp__chat.db`) rather than nesting per-app
subdirectories is deliberate: litestream names replica subdirectories after the
database filename, so `myapp/chat.db` and `other/chat.db` would replicate into
one replica prefix. Keeping the directory flat also means no Rust, no litestream
config and no db-tool changes -- `myapp__chat` already satisfies the existing
name contract.

Databases created before this keep their bare filenames. Both resolution paths
prefer the prefixed file when it exists and fall back to the bare one, so those
keep working untouched; reconcile reads the live database set inside its per-pod
lock and applies the same rule, so the file it applies DDL to is always the file
db() will open. The fallback is transitional: while it stands, two apps that
each reconcile a name which already exists unprefixed keep sharing that one
legacy database, and retiring it means renaming those files along with their
litestream replica prefixes.

An app whose folder cannot start a valid database name (`2048Game`) or whose
prefix would blow the 64-character cap falls back to unprefixed names rather
than erroring, since refusing would leave it unable to create any database at
all. Both sides apply the identical total rule, so they always agree.

@dust/pod is vendored into the sandbox image, so bump DUST_BASE_IMAGE_VERSION:
the front-side prefixing is only correct against an image carrying the matching
resolver. Deploy the image before front -- the new resolver behaves identically
until front starts creating prefixed databases, whereas front first would have
reconcile writing myapp__chat while pods still open chat.db.

* [front] chore: shrink the pod database naming surface

Three cleanups, no behavior change:

- Fold stripPodDatabasePrefix and qualifyPodDatabaseName into
  resolvePodDatabaseName. The strip only ever ran immediately before resolve, and
  qualify had no caller but resolve and its own tests, so the module exported
  three names for one decision. db_naming now exports exactly the three things
  callers need: a prefix from a slug, a prefix from a pod path, and the resolved
  name.
- Drop the dead export on podDatabasePrefixFromAppPrefix, which nothing outside
  the module referenced.
- Drop the name-contract re-check in the shim's resolveDatabasePath. A prefix too
  long to satisfy the contract is one reconcile refuses to create a file for, so
  the existence check already rejects it and the regex branch was unreachable
  weight that also duplicated front's rule.

* [front] fix: say that copying an app folder needs the Frame repointed

The database guidance claimed that keeping the app name out of the source is
"what lets an app folder be copied and get its own databases with no edit". The
databases part is true; the conclusion is not. A Frame addresses its functions by
<podId>/<slug> written into its source, so a copied folder's Frame still calls
the original app's functions and reads and writes the original's data -- the
copy's own functions and database sit published, reconciled and unused.

Narrow the claim to what actually holds (db() and the schema file never name the
app) and spell out the copy procedure, including the Frame edit. Renaming an app
folder has the same hazard.

* [front] fix: read the database prefix through podEnv, and rebump the image

Two things the rebase onto main broke.

The prefix was read straight from process.env while every other env read in
@dust/pod now goes through podEnv, which consults the per-invocation
AsyncLocalStorage context first. That context exists so a resident server can
serve concurrent invocations from different apps without touching process.env,
which is exactly the situation where a process-wide prefix is wrong: today
serve.ts still applies request env to process.env so the direct read happens to
work, but the moment it passes invocationEnv the prefix goes stale while the
databases dir and size quota beside it stay correct -- a silently wrong
database. Read it through podEnv like the rest.

The existing prefix tests could not catch this: they set process.env, and
outside a context podEnv falls back to process.env, so they pass either way.
Add three tests inside runWithInvocationEnv, including one asserting a context
without a prefix ignores the process-wide one.

Also rebump DUST_BASE_IMAGE_VERSION. 0.8.70 was the value this branch set, but
main took 0.8.70 for the group-writable-files fix while this was open, so the
rebase collapsed the bump to a no-op and the @dust/pod change here would have
shipped on an image built without it. DSBX_CLI_VERSION stays at 0.1.45: nothing
in dsbx or the runner changed here.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 * [front] Fix composer re-render storm on every keystroke Investigated per /performance, /animations, and /forms-and-inputs why clicks in the composer felt delayed. Root cause: InputBarButtons is wrapped in React.memo, but InputBarContainer passed it four inline arrow-function props (onAgentRemove, onAgentPickerOpenChange, onCapabilitiesPickerOpenChange, onAttachmentsPickerOpenChange) that were recreated on every render. Since handleEditorUpdate (registered on TipTap's "update" event, i.e. every keystroke) calls setIsEmpty and re-renders InputBarContainer, the fresh closures defeated the memo and re-rendered the entire button subtree — agent picker, capabilities picker, attachments picker, model picker, plus-menu — on every keystroke, which is exactly the kind of background work that makes clicks feel sluggish (event → paint contends with a full subtree re-render). Fixes: - Wrap those four callbacks in useCallback so InputBarButtons's memo actually holds and the button subtree stops re-rendering while typing. - handleEditorUpdate's dataSourceLink-chip sync walked the entire TipTap document with state.doc.descendants() on every keystroke regardless of whether there was anything to sync. Skip the walk when there are no attached nodes to reconcile (the common case for most messages). [front] feat: add Apps tab to Pods (#30334)

A Pod app (a Frame plus the functions and databases behind it) had no
first-class presence in the UI: apps could only be found by digging through
old conversations. This adds an Apps tab listing them.

An app stays a derived concept rather than a new record: it is a folder at
the pod root, identified by the app prefix `deriveAppPrefix` already computes
from the folder name -- the same prefix that namespaces published function
slugs and database filenames. The tab becomes a third consumer of that one
authority, so no schema, no migration, and nothing for agents to declare.

listPodApps joins three sources on that prefix in a constant number of calls:
one recursive pod file listing, one query for published functions, and one
delimited GCS list of the litestream replica prefix. Reading databases from
the replica rather than the sandbox means listing apps never wakes a sleeping
pod.

Two pre-existing ambiguities are surfaced rather than hidden: folders that
normalize onto the same prefix (`Task List` and `Task-List`) genuinely share
slugs and databases, so they are reported as one app with a warning; and
artifacts published from the pod root, which have no app folder, are collected
into an unfiled app instead of disappearing. Databases predating app
namespacing have bare filenames, so they are attributed via the schema file
that declares them, mirroring how resolvePodDatabaseName resolves the same
case at reconcile time.

Functions and databases display their bare names, since the app is already the
surrounding context; the addressable full slug and on-disk name stay on the
wire. Frames open in the existing PodFrameSheet.

Deleting an app is deliberately out of scope here and comes next.

[front] fix: namespace local sandbox image builds so CI cannot skip a region (#30365)

* [front] fix: namespace local sandbox image builds so CI cannot skip a region

The Sandbox Image Registry workflow was building an image for one region and
silently skipping the other. `sandbox_image_check.ts` decides "already built"
by asking E2B whether a template with alias `dust-base_<tag>` exists, which
assumes only CI ever creates that alias.

Nothing enforced that assumption. To exercise a locally modified image you had
to publish it under the exact alias the registry names, because
`getSandboxImage()` had no dev override. `sandbox_image_build.ts` then refuses
to overwrite an existing alias without --rebuild, so the path of least
resistance while iterating was to bump DUST_BASE_IMAGE_VERSION again. That
burned release numbers ahead of main: EU held dust-base_0-8-74 through
0-8-78 while none of those versions existed in any commit. When main later

[front] feat: delete a Pod app (#30375)

Completes the other half of the Apps tab: an app can now be deleted, along
with everything it owns.

`deletePodApp` returns a domain error and the handler maps it to HTTP, so the
business layer stays transport-agnostic per BACK18.

The step order is the design, fixed by two constraints. Functions are
unpublished first, so no invocation can arrive while the data underneath it is
being removed. And a database's live files go before its replica, because a
running litestream re-replicates a database it can still see — the same hazard
the pod-scrub path already notes.

The source folder goes last on purpose. Every step is idempotent, and the
folder is what makes the app appear in the Apps tab, so a failure part-way
through leaves the app still listed and simply re-deletable. Deleting the
folder first would instead leave an invisible half-deleted app.

Wiping a replica is verified by re-listing, because a silently-surviving
replica is indistinguishable from success until the pod next boots — at which
point cold-start restore would bring the database back. Deleting databases
needs a live sandbox, so a sleeping pod is woken (execDbCommand already does
it) and the dialog says so rather than showing a bare spinner.

Removing the live database files is a plain rm that front builds, run through
the existing execDbCommand path, rather than a new dsbx subcommand. dsbx is the
agent-facing CLI, so a destructive database primitive there would be
discoverable from inside the sandbox; this adds no such surface, and grants no
new capability either since the databases dir is already group-writable by
`agent`. It also keeps front free of any dsbx version coupling. The name is
validated with isValidPodDatabaseName, the same guard the replica path uses.

The confirmation names what goes — functions, databases, Frames and file count
— and warns separately about unrecoverable data and about published Frame
links that will break. Deletion is refused for the synthetic unfiled app,
which is a presentation device rather than a folder.

No audit event yet: pod_app.deleted comes in a follow-up, so this does not
have to carry a WorkOS schema registration.

[front] feat: resolve app-relative pod function references in the Frame host (#30397)

* [front] feat: resolve app-relative pod function references in the Frame host

Groundwork for cloning and renaming Pod apps. A Frame addresses its functions by
a fully qualified `<podId>/<slug>` written into its source, and the slug carries
the app prefix — so a copied app's Frame keeps calling the ORIGINAL app's
functions, and therefore reads and writes the original's data. The pod functions
skill documents that trap today and asks the model to hand-edit every reference
after a copy.

This adds a second reference form: a bare `<name>` with no `/`, resolved against
the app folder the calling Frame lives in. `list-notes` inside
`pod-x/TaskList/TaskList.tsx` means `pod-x/tasklist__list-notes`, so the same
source follows whichever app it ends up in. Absolute references are untouched
and stay the only way to name a function in another Pod.

Resolution happens in the host that renders the Frame, because that is the only
layer that both knows which Frame is calling and is trusted about it: the Frame
does not know its own path, and the invocation request carries no Frame
identity. Publish-time rewriting was the other candidate and does not work — an
unpublished Frame renders its source, so relative references would break exactly
while the app is being written.

Only Pod hosts pass a frame path, so only a Frame inside an app folder gets a
scope. A Frame at the Pod root or in a conversation resolves to none and its
bare references are refused with a clear error, which is what confines the
relative form to apps.

`normalizeAppPrefix` moves to a client-safe module so the host and publish derive
the prefix with the same function; if they disagreed, a Frame would resolve to a
function that does not exist. A test pins that agreement against
deriveSandboxFunctionSlug.

Inert on its own: viz still rejects the bare form, so nothing can use it yet.
A test pins that too, because a reference viz rejects becomes a null SWR key and
the Frame silently issues no request at all — the failure mode this rollout
order exists to avoid. Widening the viz grammar is step 2; teaching the skill to
emit relative references is step 3 and is what turns adoption on.

* fix: give shared and conversation-hosted Frames their app scope

A Frame in an app folder only resolved bare function references when opened
from the Pod. Shared at /share/frame/<token> it failed with "a bare function
name only works from a Frame that lives in an app folder" — the Frame does live
in one; the share host just had no way to know.

Three hosts render a Pod Frame and each needed its own answer:

- FrameRenderer (conversation side panel) already computed a framePath from the
  pod file listing and simply never passed it on. One line.
- PublicFrameRenderer (share) had nothing to derive from: the public response
  returns a FileType, which carries neither a path nor useCaseMetadata. It now
  carries the Frame's scoped path.
- The Pod hosts were already wired.

The new field is withheld from viewers who cannot read the Pod. They cannot
invoke a pod function either, so sending it would hand out the Pod's layout for
nothing — and with relative references the Frame's own source no longer reveals
the pod id, so this keeps that closed. Additive and optional on a public
endpoint, per BACK12.

Also adds mountFilePath to FileFactory, since a file needs one to have a scoped
path at all and production assigns it while copying into the mount.
[front,sparkle] fix: prevent panel content reflow during open/close animations (#28440)

[viz] feat: accept app-relative pod function references (#30400)

Step 2 of making Pod apps copyable. Front already resolves a bare function
name against the app folder the calling Frame lives in; viz still rejects that
form, so nothing can reach the resolver yet. This widens the grammar.

A reference is now either the fully qualified `<podId>/<slug>`, unchanged and
still the only form that can name a function in another Pod, or a bare `<name>`
that the host qualifies against the Frame's own app folder.

The two forms stay separate patterns rather than one with an optional
`<podId>/`, because that would also admit a prefixed-but-podless
`tasklist__list-notes` — and dropping the prefix is the entire point of the
relative form. `isPodFunctionReference` is the single predicate the hook uses,
so viz decides only whether a reference is well formed; deciding what it means
belongs to the host, which is the layer that knows which Frame is calling.

This matters because a reference viz rejects resolves to a null SWR key, so the
Frame silently issues no request at all. viz therefore has to accept exactly
what front is willing to resolve, and the front-side test now asserts that
agreement string for string instead of pinning the old rejection.

Still nothing emits relative references: teaching the pod functions skill to
use them is step 3, and that is what turns adoption on.

[front] enh: teach the pod functions skill app-relative references (#30403)

Step 3, and the one that turns adoption on: front resolves relative references
and viz forwards them, but nothing emits them until the skill says to.

A Frame inside an app folder now refers to its own app's functions by bare name
— the same name passed to publish, with no Pod and no app prefix — because that
reference resolves against whichever app folder the Frame ends up in. Fully
qualified `<podId>/<slug>` stays required for reaching another app or another
Pod, and for any Frame that does not live in an app folder.

That turns the copy warning from a four-step correction into a note. Copying an
app still needs its functions published and its databases reconciled, but the
Frame no longer has to be rewritten, which was the step whose omission silently
left the copy reading and writing the ORIGINAL app's data. The warning now
covers only the case that still bites: a Frame that hard-codes its own app's
prefix.

Also corrects the publish section, which told the model to use the reported slug
"everywhere afterwards, and a Frame's reference" — now true of the addressing
tools only, with the in-app Frame called out as the exception. And states plainly
that a prefixed-but-podless `tasklist__add-task` is not shorthand and is refused,
since that is the mistake the two forms invite.

[front] feat: clone a Pod app (#30410)

* [front] feat: clone a Pod app (business layer)

Copies an app into a new folder in the same Pod: every file under the folder,
its functions re-published under the copy's prefix, and its databases
reconciled from the copied schema files as fresh empty ones. Database rows,
share tokens, the pinned tab and invocation history deliberately do not carry
over, and the copy's Frame is left unpublished so the author decides when it
becomes a shareable artifact.

Frames need their own path. A Frame copied as a bare GCS object has no
FileResource, so it cannot be published or shared and surfaces with a null file
id — which is why the files MCP server refuses to copy Frames at all. Every
other file is copied directly; Frames are recreated through a new
createPodFrameFile, composed from public steps: uploadContent claims the Pod
mount path, which always lands at the Pod root, then the file is moved into its
folder. That move is what makes the Frame belong to the app, and therefore what
makes its bare function references resolve against it.

Nothing rewrites the copied Frame's source. One that names its functions by
bare name is correct by construction; one that hard-codes
`<podId>/<prefix>__<name>` keeps calling the original app's functions, and its
author fixes that themselves.

Collision is checked on the normalized prefix rather than the folder name, since
two names that normalize alike would share published slugs and databases.
Functions or databases whose source the copy does not have are reported as
skipped rather than failing the clone.

Endpoint and UI follow.

* [front] feat: add the clone endpoint and Apps tab action

Wires clonePodApp up: POST /apps/:prefix/clone, a useClonePodApp hook, and a
Clone action in the app detail pane.

The dialog validates the new name against the normalized prefix rather than the
folder name, because that is what has to be unique — two names that normalize
alike would share published slugs and databases — and it shows the prefix the
functions will carry so the result is not a surprise.

It also says what a clone does not copy. The databases come from the same schema
but hold no data, the Frame is left unpublished, and a Frame that spells out
`<podId>/<prefix>__<name>` keeps calling the original app's functions until its
author changes those references. That last one is the trap relative references
removed for new Frames, so the dialog names it rather than letting it be
discovered later.

Cloning is synchronous and rebuilds every function on the Pod's Computer, so the
busy state says so instead of implying it is quick.

* fix: pass a relative path when moving a cloned Frame into its folder

Cloning failed with "No such object:
.../pods/{podId}/files/pod-{podId}/AnimalManager.tsx" — the Pod scope prefix
ended up nested inside the GCS mount path.

`createPodFrameFile` handed `moveProjectFile` the canonical scoped path from
`toScopedPath`. That function does accept a scoped source, but only the legacy
`pod/...` form: `parseScopedFilePath` does not recognise the canonical
`pod-{podId}/...`, so the whole string fell through to the relative-path branch
and was appended to the mount base. It now derives the relative path explicitly.

Extracted as podRelativePathFromScopedPath and unit tested, because that
derivation is where the mistake was. The clone endpoint test that would have
caught it end to end is not viable: creating a Frame goes through
uploadContent, which never settles under the file-storage mock, so the
integration path stays a manual check.

* review: index the copy's function sources by name

Matching each published function to its copied source scanned every copied file
and rebuilt an array of the map's keys on each pass. Building the index once
turns the lookup into a Map.get.

The complexity was never going to bite — a handful of functions against a few
dozen files — but the indexed version reads better than a three-clause `find`
predicate inline in the loop, and it drops the per-iteration array. It also
stores the destination path directly, so the loop no longer looks the same key
up twice.

* [front] enh: drop the Frame-references warning from the clone dialog

The dialog warned that a Frame spelling out `<podId>/<prefix>__<name>` would
keep calling the source app's functions. Relative references are how Frames are
written now, so the warning describes a case that should not arise and only adds
noise to the one decision the dialog exists for: the new app's name.

* Reuse constant

* review: simplify the clone's path bookkeeping and result types

Two things carrying more weight than they earned.

`copiedPathByRelPath` was a Map whose every value was `{destFolderPath}/{key}`
— information the key already had. It was also built in a second pass over the
same entries the copy loop had just walked, and it included the Frames, which
that loop deliberately skips because they are recreated rather than copied. Now
the copy loop records the relative paths it actually copied, and destination
paths are formed where they are used.

The clone and delete summaries were each declared twice: once as a result type
in the business layer, once inline in the response body. They are the same shape
by definition — the endpoint returns the result verbatim — so they are declared
once in types/api and the business layer aliases them, which also means they can
no longer drift.
