[front] enh: clean up Pod app listing — namespaced databases only, no Unfiled app (#30423)

* [front] enh: list only namespaced databases in the Apps tab

A database created before app namespacing has a bare filename, which says
nothing about which app owns it. The tab inferred ownership from the schema file
that declares it — and that inference stops being reliable as soon as apps can
be copied, because a copy inherits the declaration while opening its own
prefixed file. Cloning Counter into Counter Copy made both apps list two
databases called `counter`.

Rather than sharpen the inference, drop it: only namespaced databases are
listed. Grouping goes from a filter over declaring folders to a lookup on the
filename, and the machinery that fed it goes with it — the declared-names set on
each app folder, the pass that read `databases/*.db.ts` to populate it, and the
schema-file suffix constant.

Two consequences, accepted deliberately and documented where the decision lives:
an app whose only database predates namespacing now shows none even though the
runtime still opens that file, and deleting such an app leaves the database and
its replica behind, since delete works from this listing.

Both disappear once bare databases are migrated to their prefixed names, which
is also what allows the step 2 fallback in resolvePodDatabaseName to be removed.

Two leftovers from the tab's first version.

had somewhere to appear. With unprefixed databases no longer listed, keeping it
for functions alone was inconsistent, and it was never an app: it had no folder,
could not be deleted, and every consumer had to special-case a prefix that is
the empty string. A prefix-less function stays published and callable; it simply
has no app to be listed under.

Removing it lets `PodApp.name` stop being nullable, which was only nullable for
that one synthetic entry. That in turn removes the `?? "Unfiled"` fallbacks in
both components, the empty-prefix guard in delete along with its error code and
the endpoint case that mapped it, and a `removeNulls` around a value that can no
longer be null.

The detail pane also showed the app's scoped path under its name
(`pod-{podId}/AnimalManager`). The pod id is not information the reader needs and
the folder name is already the heading, so the line is gone.

Clone landed while this branch was open and carried the empty-prefix guard the

the route's prefix param requires at least one character — so it goes along with

feat(sandbox): resolve conversation scope inside the lifecycle lock (#30386)

* feat(sandbox): resolve conversation scope inside the lifecycle lock

The pod association is an authorization input (egress claims, pod env
vars, pod mounts) and was derived from state read before the lifecycle
lock — so a move committing between that read and the lock acquisition
could create or wake a sandbox in its pre-move pod. The adapter now
resolves the conversation's spaceId from the database as the first step
inside the locked section, the env-var factory receives that resolved
scope, and ensureActive returns it so the ready path derives the
filesystem, runtime owner, and egress claims from it. Callers'
conversation objects are trusted for identity only; the type no longer
accepts a caller-provided spaceId.

Pods resolve a constant scope (they cannot move), which also keeps
requireRunning's lock-free fast path sound.

A scope transition (conversation move) holds the same lock, so once
moves destroy strictly under it, no interleaving can produce a sandbox
whose runtime state predates a committed move.

* fix(sandbox): give the lifecycle lock a TTL that outlives the operations it serializes

executeWithLock's lease defaults to 5 seconds while provider create and
wake take seconds to minutes — an expired lease lets a concurrent ensure
(or scope transition) acquire the lock mid-operation, silently voiding
the serialization every lifecycle path depends on. The lease is now 5
minutes, sized to the slowest locked operation; a crashed holder strands
the lock for at most that long, and waiters give up at the 30s
acquisition timeout well before. A renewable lease is the durable fix
(dated TODO).

* docs(sandbox): state the fixed lock TTL as a decision, not a deferral

The renewable-lease TODO implied follow-up work we have no intention of
doing absent evidence: the comment now records the trade-off and what
would reopen it.

feat(sandbox): lock-scoped conversation scope resolution + strict sandbox destroy on moves (#30379)

* feat(sandbox): strict sandbox destroy under the lifecycle lock on conversation moves

Moving a conversation now runs as a scope transition: one lifecycle-lock
hold covers the strict provider destroy, marking the sandbox deleted,
and the database association change. Combined with scope resolution
under the same lock (previous commit), a concurrent Computer command can
neither keep a pre-move sandbox alive nor create one from the pre-move
scope; its next invocation recreates the sandbox in place — new egress
claims, pod env vars, and mounts — via the existing deleted-state path.

Recovery uses only existing machinery: killRequestedAt is set before the
provider call, so a crash at any point (or a failed destroy, which fails
the move) leaves the kill-requested branch or the reaper to finish the
reset, and the conversation's next access always rebuilds from whichever
association actually committed. Environments without a sandbox provider
run the transition with a vacuous runtime destroy.

The sandbox row and owner association survive (recreate-in-place), as do
the conversation's egress policy file and GCS files.

* fix(front): teach the mock redis client the distributed-lock contract

distributedLock acquires with SET NX PX and treats anything but "OK" as
failure — the global mock's set returned undefined, so any suite calling
executeWithLock (the sandbox scope-transition path) spun the acquire
loop until its 30s timeout and hit the test timeout. set now honors
NX/PX against the store and returns "OK"; the stateful client's eval
implements the unlock script's compare-and-delete so sequential lock
cycles within a suite work.

* fix(sandbox): validate scope transitions under the lock, against lock-fetched state

Addresses review on the strict-destroy design:

- runScopeTransition becomes two-phase: prepare (re-read + validate
  against current state) runs under the lock BEFORE the destroy — an
  Err aborts with the runtime untouched, so a rejected move can no
  longer grief the sandbox — and commit runs after it. The conversation
  wrapper re-fetches the conversation under the lock and hands it to
  both callbacks; the caller's object is identity-only.
- Both move functions validate their source pod against the lock-fetched
  conversation, closing the race where two concurrent moves both
  validate against the same stale source.
- The outer-transaction parameter is gone: the move's transaction is
  always created and committed inside the lock hold — a commit deferred
  past the lock release would reopen the race the lock closes.
- Failures are typed (ConversationGoneError, ScopeTransitionDestroyError)
  so the moves map them to their error unions without casts.

* fix(front): scope the mock-redis lock fix to the set return value only

The previous commit made the shared mock enforce SET NX and gave eval
compare-and-delete semantics — but eval is script-dependent (the rate
limiter's Lua scripts need their numeric result, which broke OTP and
message quota suites with spurious 429/403s) and NX enforcement changes
consumers that legitimately re-set live keys. Tests run sequentially,
so the lock never needs mutual exclusion to actually hold: returning
"OK" from set is the entire requirement for executeWithLock to work
against the mock.

[sparkle][front] Highlight the model picker for discovery (#30402)

* [sparkle][front] Highlight the model picker for discovery

Temporary treatment drawing attention to the model picker: a blue ring that
pulses twice every 7s, two diagonal light streaks sweeping across right after
each pulse, and one extra sweep on hover. Values come from the Figma —
Blue/200 ring at radius 8, Blue/50 streaks 3px wide at 30° with a 1px blur.

Pulse and sweep share one 7s animation each, with the active part expressed
as a percentage of that duration, so the streaks always follow the pulse
instead of drifting out of step the way two hand-matched delays would.

Both ends of the streaks' travel sit clear of the box, so they are never
parked over the button — the effect only exists while it is moving. Only
`transform` is animated, on layers that are absolutely positioned and
pointer-events-none, so the button's box, layout and hit area are untouched
and removing the wrapper shifts nothing.

Clicking the picker retires the highlight for the rest of the visit;
useModelPickerHighlight caps it at two page loads per browser, spending the
count per load rather than per click so a user who never clicks still stops
seeing it. Under prefers-reduced-motion the streaks and the pulse are
dropped and the static ring carries the highlight alone.

Wrapped inside InputBarModelPicker rather than at its call sites, so both
input bar surfaces get it while the model pickers in the agent builder and
app blocks stay untouched.

* [front] Fix the model picker highlight never dismissing on click

Clicking the picker was supposed to retire the highlight for the rest of the
visit, and it never did.

Radix opens the dropdown on `pointerdown` and, being modal, sets
`pointer-events: none` on the body. The mouseup that follows therefore
hit-tests to <html> rather than to the button, so the browser dispatches the
click there and no click event ever reaches the highlight's subtree. Listen on

primary button to match Radix's own condition for opening.

The original check passed because it drove the button with `element.click()`,

one part of the sequence that was broken. Re-verified by replaying the real
sequence: pointerdown on the button, then mouseup wherever the browser

[front] fix: restart litestream when a Pod app's databases are deleted (#30490)

Deleting an app removed a database's live files and then wiped its replica prefix, on the assumption
that a litestream that can no longer see the files stops replicating them. It does not: the
directory watcher only enumerates /pod-state/databases at start, so until the daemon restarts it
still holds the deleted database open and can recreate the prefix the wipe just removed. The
replica-wipe verification is a point-in-time re-listing, so a prefix that comes back seconds later
looks like success — and the pod's next cold start restores the database from it.

So `deletePodApp` now restarts the daemon between the two steps: remove every live file, restart,
then wipe every replica. One restart rather than one per database, which still satisfies the
per-database ordering the wipe depends on. A failed restart aborts before any replica is touched;
the whole flow is idempotent, so the app stays listed and is simply re-deletable.

`restartLitestreamDaemon` lands in sandbox/db.ts next to the start helper, and the pre-sleep sync
recovery in `ensurePodStateHealthOnSleep` uses it instead of its own inline systemctl call. Its
default budget is 120s because a restart waits out the stop half, and litestream's graceful shutdown
syncs every managed database before exiting — seconds normally, up to the unit's 90s
TimeoutStopSec when one of them cannot reach its replica. The pre-sleep caller keeps the tight probe
budget it has today, since it runs inside the reaper's per-batch budget and its next cycle retries
the whole check anyway.

feat(dsbx): resolve offloaded tool output under `tools --json`

Tool results above front's 20KB text threshold are archived to the pod
filesystem and delivered as an 8KB snippet plus a "[Full content archived
at ...]" sentence, with a machine-readable descriptor in the block's
`_meta` ("tt.dust/offload"). That truncation protects a model's context
window, but `--json` is a machine contract with no model on the other
end, so it was emitting bodies that do not parse (a 121,700-byte result
arrived as an 8,157-byte fragment).

Under `--json` only, read the archive back from the /files mount and
substitute it into the block text (resource.text, or top-level text),
with the same bounded retry as the pod TypeScript helper for gcsfuse
metadata staleness. On exhaustion it fails with a typed error in the
existing stdout error envelope (code tool_output_unavailable, exit 15)
rather than silently emitting the truncated snippet.

Default mode is unchanged: it is model-facing and keeps the snippet plus
the archive sentence.

Harden offload resolution after review

- Confine the archive path to the /files mount: `_meta` is not fully
  trusted (front passes some remote MCP resource blocks through
  verbatim), so a forged descriptor should not aim the read elsewhere.
- Retry only NotFound. Permissions or non-UTF-8 content are terminal and
  were burning the 5s retry budget with a misleading message.
- Drop the descriptor from the resolved block: it means "the inline text
  is a snippet", which stops being true after substitution and would make
  a downstream resolver read the file again.
- Private `mod offload`, `super::` import, exit_code_for coverage.

A section on the shared egress policy schema recording domains an agent
asked to reach, pending admin approval — the proxy ignores unknown
fields, so only allowedDomains is authorization state and this section
is admin-workflow state riding along for atomic approve transitions.

- writeOwnerPolicy and writeWorkspacePolicy both preserve the section, so
  replacing the allowlist never wipes pending requests, and appending an
  approved domain resolves its request in one write (normalize drops

  dismissRequestedWorkspacePolicyDomain remove one without granting. Both
  scopes share one core (requestPolicyDomain / dismissRequestedPolicyDomain
  over a read/write pair). Exact domains or wildcards; deduped against
  allowed and pending; capped at 50 (the proxy re-reads the file on cache
  misses).

audit-log territory if ever needed, not stored here.

[front] feat: change pod_editor_required to pod_member_required (#30583)

* [dsbx] feat: accept the pod_member_required user identity policy in the functions-runner

* [front] feat: pod_member_required identity policy for Pod Functions

New Pod Function policy filling the tier between workspace_user_required and
pod_editor_required:

- pod_member_required authorizes a workspace member who belongs to any of the
  pod's groups (member or editor — a user is never in both), plus workspace
  admins via their role, so its audience is a strict superset of
  pod_editor_required's. canRead would not do: open pods grant read to the
  whole workspace, so it cannot separate members from bystanders.
- Publish strength ranks it above the session-bound policy and below
  pod_editor_required, so a publish moving to a pod-scoped policy always
  commits the policy before exposing the new bundle.
- The publish tool description now lists all five policies (it had not been
  updated for pod_editor_required).

Requires the dsbx runner change accepting the policy string to be deployed
first, otherwise publishes declaring it throw at build.

* [front] fix: pod_member_required denies workspace admins outside the pod

Membership now means exactly the pod's groups (member or editor), the people
who hold write on the pod and can publish its functions. Workspace admins
outside those groups hold admin but not write on projects, so they cannot
publish pod functions — treating them as members would grant invocation to
callers with no standing in the pod. This differs from pod_editor_required,
which keys on canAdministrate, a capability admins do hold.

* [dsbx] feat: retire the pod_editor_required user identity policy in the functions-runner

* [front] feat: retire the pod_editor_required identity policy

The editor tier was not a meaningful boundary: pod members hold write on the
pod and can republish any function (restating its policy), so gating
invocation on editorship never withstood a member anyway. Editor-only
behavior inside a function remains possible through the identity envelope's
isPodEditor, which stays.

Stored rows that still carry the retired value fail closed at invocation
(the authorizer's default branch denies unknown policies) and are repaired by
republishing: userIdentityPolicyStrength now ranks unknown stored values
strictest instead of throwing, so a republish over a retired policy succeeds
and overwrites it.

* [front] feat: isPodMember in the Frame identity state and invocation envelope

A Frame gating UI on a pod_member_required function had no way to know whether
the viewer would pass it — in an open pod, non-members can view the Frame and
would only discover the gate by calling the function and getting denied.

Mirrors what b448e12f68 did for isPodEditor:

- The invocation identity envelope carries isPodMember (space.isMember, the
  same predicate as pod_member_required and the pod UI's isMember);
  currentUser() in @dust/pod exposes it, absent meaning false so old
  envelopes still parse.
- Frames: UserIdentityState gains a display-only isPodMember; pod hosts
  (frame tabs, pinned banner, frame sheet) thread the pod's isMember into the
  scoped identity; other hosts and the public cache answer false. Old hosts
  that omit the field normalize to false in the viz RPC data API.

viz must deploy before front, as usual for changes spanning both.

* Bump dsbx to 0.1.50 and dust-base to 0.8.84

dsbx picks up the functions-runner accepting pod_member_required (and dropping
pod_editor_required); dust-base re-vendors @dust/pod so currentUser() exposes
isPodMember.

* Remove log line

* [front] docs: state why the unknown-policy branches use assertNeverAndIgnore

The stored policy is cross-revision data, not internal control flow: throwing
would 500 invocations in workspace_user.ts and, in the strength ranking, make
a function carrying a retired policy permanently unrepairable (republish is
the only path that rewrites the stored value).

* [front] feat: export a Pod app as a portable zip archive

Adds GET /:prefix/export on the Pod apps routes, packaging the app folder's
files under files/ plus a manifest.json carrying publish metadata (function
descriptions/execution modes, Frame publish state and pinned-tab info,
per-file content types) so the archive can be re-imported anywhere.

* [front] feat: import a Pod app archive into any pod

Adds the import half of Pod app portability: importPodApp() unpacks a
.podapp.zip archive (validating manifest, entries and size before touching
the pod), recreates its Frames, republishes its functions and databases
under the destination folder, and republishes any Frames that were
published at export time. Exposes it at POST /api/w/:wId/pods/:podId/apps/import.

construct/match on it (needed to test the Frame-publish-warning path).

* [front] fix: body-limit gate, tab-pin coverage, and sandbox_unavailable docs for Pod app import

Addresses task-2 review findings:
- Gate the multipart body with the existing bodyLimit(...) middleware sized to
  MAX_POD_APP_ARCHIVE_SIZE_BYTES plus a small multipart-framing allowance, so an oversized
  upload is rejected before ctx.req.parseBody() buffers it. Without a Content-Length header the
  middleware signals the overflow by erroring the request stream mid-read; let that specific
  error propagate out of the route instead of reporting it as a generic 400 parse failure, so the
  middleware's own onError still produces the 413.
- Add coverage for importPodApp's tab-pinning path: a clean pin that updates ProjectMetadata's
  frameTabs/tabsOrder, and a pin attempt at MAX_POD_FRAME_TABS that warns instead of pinning and
  leaves metadata untouched.
- Fix the importPodApp docstring: a sandbox_unavailable abort leaves the partial app (folder,
  any Frames already created) visible in the Apps tab; retrying the same import hits name_taken
  rather than resuming, so recovery means deleting the partial app first or finishing it in
  place. Add a test asserting the route returns 503 on sandbox_unavailable.

Adds a Download action to each PodAppTile and an ImportPodAppDialog reachable

* [front] fix: keep ImportPodAppDialog mounted across the empty-to-populated apps transition

PodAppsTab rendered ImportPodAppDialog at different tree positions in its
empty-state and populated-state returns, so the first-ever import into an
empty pod (which flips apps.length 0->1) unmounted and remounted the dialog

Addresses final whole-branch review findings for Pod app import/export:

[front] feat: default stake on published pod functions (#30626)

* [front] feat: default stake on published pod functions

Sharing a pod function as an MCP tool will need to know how much approval it
should require. Record that at publish time, while the model that wrote the
function still knows what it does, rather than guessing later from its name or
its schema.

`defaultStake` is a subset of MCP_TOOL_STAKE_LEVELS (never_ask / low / high),
declared `satisfies readonly MCPToolStakeLevelType[]` so sharing needs no
translation. `medium` is excluded: it only means anything paired with
`argumentsRequiringApproval`, which a published function has no way to declare.

The column is NOT NULL DEFAULT 'low', and the publish argument is optional and
falls back to the same constant, so functions published before today ask once
instead of running unattended. Like the execution mode, the stake is restated by
every publish rather than carried forward, so a function that grows a
destructive path cannot keep the `never_ask` it earned while it was a read.

The app archive manifest field is optional at the same format version, so
archives exported before this change still import.

Nothing gates on the stake yet; the skill guidance that teaches the model to set
it, and making the publish argument required, come next.

* [front] feat: require a default stake on every publish

The stake was optional against the `low` fallback. In a fresh context the model
sets it correctly from the argument description, but an optional field is the
one that gets skipped when publishing the fifth function in a long context —
and a read-only function that silently lands on `low` then prompts the user for
approval forever, with nothing recording that the stake was defaulted rather
than chosen.

Required removes the mode instead of making it unlikely, and matches
`executionMode`, which is required on the tool for the same reason.

`publishSandboxFunction` keeps its optional parameter: an app archive exported
before stakes existed carries no stake, and that path still needs the fallback.

* fix(front): also display skills used in UsedBy button

* perf(front): scope the skill-usage fetch by data source ids

`fetchSkillsByDataSource` loaded every active skill in the workspace via
`listByWorkspace`, then bucketed them in memory. Four usage functions rely on
it, and two (`getDataSourceViewUsage`, `getDataSourceUsage`) are called inside
loops — the space-deletion guard in `spaces.ts` ran it once per view and per
data source, making it O(views x all workspace skills) full hydrations.

Add `SkillResource.listByDataSourceIds` next to the existing
`listByDataSourceViewIds`, following the same shape as `listByMCPServerViewIds`:
start from `skill_data_source_configurations` (both columns are indexed
alongside `workspaceId`) so only the skills actually referencing the requested
ids get loaded. Both data source methods now expose the hydration flags so the
caller decides; usage passes all three false, since it only reads sId/name/icon
(`dataSourceConfigurations` and `editorGroup` are loaded unconditionally by
`baseFetch` regardless).

All four call sites now pass an explicit id list. `getDataSourcesUsageByCategory`
is the only one without ids in hand, so it resolves them with one query using
the `connectorProvider` it already computes. `mergeSkillsIntoUsage`'s
`allowedIds` param is dropped — the query does that scoping now.

Side effect: `getDataSourcesUsageByCategory` previously merged skills
workspace-wide, so a "folder" query returned extra keys for website/managed data
sources with skill usage. It is now correctly scoped to the requested category;
its only caller reads just the keys for views it already holds, so nothing
visible changes.

Note: most of the diff in agent_data_sources.ts is re-indentation — collapsing
the destructuring to one line shifted the Promise.all bodies. Review with
whitespace hidden.

* [front] feat: search automations by name in the analytics table

The filter panel covers agent, editor and type, but finding one automation
among hundreds still means paging through the table. Adds a name search on
the filters row, applied to the credit-ranked buckets rather than the
Elasticsearch query so that it narrows the rows without rescoping the median

* [front] refactor: resolve the automations search in SQL, keep ranking in ES

The first pass read every trigger in the workspace to match names in memory and
moved ranking and pagination out of Elasticsearch, which lost the terms
aggregation's deterministic tie-break: credit ties could put a trigger on two
pages or none at all.

search resolves to a set of trigger ids with an ILIKE, the way the kind filter
already resolves its own, and applies to the ranked buckets rather than to the
query, so the median baseline keeps comparing a row against every trigger that
ran. listByWorkspaceAndKinds comes back instead of filtering kinds in memory.

[dsbx] pod: tools.call() delegates to dsbx tools --json

The POST+poll transport, its retry policy, and offloaded-output resolution
now live in exactly one place, the dsbx CLI. @dust/pod's tools.call() spawns
dsbx tools --json --args-json - asynchronously (args over stdin, so no argv
limits and no scalar coercion) and parses the stdout contract: the result
payload on completion, the typed error envelope on transport failure.
ToolCallError codes now mirror the CLI's append-only envelope contract, with
unrecognized future codes degrading to unknown while keeping the envelope's
message and retryable flag.

Address review: bounded pipe drain, timeout grace, offload doc accuracy

The exit-then-drain path is now under the same deadline as the exit wait, so
a pipe held open by a stray descendant of an exited child throws timeout
instead of hanging. The default timeout gains a 30s grace over dsbx's poll
ceiling so dsbx's typed envelope wins at the default. The module docstring
no longer claims offload resolution unconditionally: it requires a dsbx
newer than the currently pinned 0.1.49.

neither had a `long_context` pricing entry, so prompts above 272K input
tokens were billed at the short-context rate.

Per the model docs, prompts with >272K input tokens are priced at 2x
input and 1.5x output for the full request (cached input scales 2x
alongside input, matching the published gpt-5.6-* long-context tables):

- https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-5.5
- https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-5.4

EU pricing picks up the new tiers automatically through
`applyRegionalUplift`, as both model IDs are already in
EU_UPLIFT_MODEL_IDS.

[front] Log non-integer credit deltas in spend-limit rate-cap recorders

The three fixed-window spend-cap recorders (per-user, per-API-key,
programmatic) silently `return` on a non-integer `incrementBy` before it

weights, stored in an INTEGER column), so this must never fire; log it as an
error with workspace context if it ever does. Keep the non-positive case
silent since a 0 delta is a normal no-op (retry with no new usage).

To preselect the flag, `PluginForm` (and `RunPluginDialog`) take an optional `initialValues` map, merged over the manifest defaults for declared args only. * [front] Add legacy flag cleanup and per-workspace flag toggling to Poke

Adds a Delete Legacy Feature Flag global plugin: it lists only the flag names still present in the database but no longer declared in WHITELISTABLE_FEATURES_CONFIG (with their workspace count), refuses a name that still exists in the codebase, and deletes every row for the one selected. Legacy rows in the feature flags table get a "Delete rows" button that opens it preselected.

On the flag detail page, each workspace row gets a "Toggle flags" button that opens that workspace's Toggle Feature Flag plugin. The plugin list depends on the workspace (maintenance mode, per-plugin applicability), so it is fetched once the workspace is known. The plugin is opened without prefilled arguments on purpose: it applies the full set of flags it is given and disables everything left unchecked, and its own async arguments already check exactly the flags the workspace has today.

- `FeatureFlagResource.deleteLegacyByName` bulk-deleted without the workspace isolation bypass, so it threw outside production and never invalidated the per-workspace flag cache. Per [BACK5], `lib/api/poke/feature_flags.ts` no longer imports Sequelize models. `FeatureFlagResource` gains the two cross-workspace readers the poke pages need — `countByFlagNameForAllWorkspaces` and `listForAllWorkspacesByName` — and the workspace names now come from `WorkspaceResource.fetchByModelIds` instead of an inline join, so the lib layer only talks to Resources.

feat(agent_inactivity): add inactive agent archival business rules (#30777)

First brick of the opt-in "automatically archive inactive agents" feature:
the business rules and the use case that applies them. The database query
is deliberately deferred — the use case carries the whole flow with the
fetch marked as a TODO where it belongs.

- inactivity/policy.ts: domain rules. Pure — no database, Temporal, HTTP or
  Authenticator. Threshold validation (integer, 2 days minimum, no implicit
  default), cutoff resolution, and per-agent eligibility with
  machine-readable exclusion reasons.
- inactivity/archive_inactive_agents.ts: the use case. Resolves the policy
  into a cutoff, loads the workspace's agents, and for each one re-reads the
  facts the decision depends on, applies the rules, and archives it through
  the existing archiveAgentConfiguration primitive.

The rules are applied against state read immediately before the mutation
rather than against the loaded page, because the page ages while it is
processed: an agent can be restored, archived by someone else, or given a
schedule in the meantime. That is also what makes a Temporal retry safe —
replaying the same input re-reads an agent the first attempt archived, sees
archived, and skips it instead of emitting a second agent.archived audit
event.

An invalid threshold is returned as an Err for the whole operation rather
than as a per-agent exclusion, so a misconfigured workspace can never be
mistaken for "no agent to archive".

The cutoff is a day boundary, not an instant: the threshold is expressed in
whole days, so a nightly run at 02:00 and an admin previewing at 17:00 judge
every agent identically, and an agent cannot become eligible partway through
a day. Truncating to the start of the UTC day only ever grants more grace
than the threshold asks for, never less.

Activity is read from mentions rather than agent messages: mention rows
carry the stable agent sId with no configuration version, their createdAt is
never null, and (workspaceId, agentConfigurationId, createdAt) is already
indexed. Any mention counts, whatever became of the run it started.

Agent status is modelled as AgentConfigurationStatus rather than
AgentStatus, because reading a configuration back surfaces the global-agent
statuses (disabled_by_admin, disabled_free_workspace,
disabled_missing_datasource). The rules reject them explicitly: a workspace
policy has no business retiring an agent it does not own.

feat(agent_inactivity): fetch inactive agent candidates from mentions  (#30858)

* [front] feat: fetch inactive agent candidates from mentions

Gives the archival use case its data, so the flow runs end to end: one page
of the workspace's agents that have not been mentioned since the cutoff.

- resources/mention_resource.ts: MentionModel had no Resource.
  `listAgentsNotMentionedSince` is the query, driven by the agents with
  mentions as an anti-join — the set we want is defined by absence, and an
  agent nobody ever mentioned has no row in `mentions` at all, so no query
  selecting from that table could return it.
- inactivity/fetch_inactive_agents.ts: the paging contract over that query.
- archiveInactiveWorkspaceAgents takes { cursor, limit } and returns
  nextCursor, so the caller owns the loop — the nightly workflow one durable
  step at a time, a manual run until its own budget runs out.

The cursor is load-bearing for agents the rules keep refusing. Archiving
removes an agent from the candidate set, so that path is self-consuming, but
an agent with an enabled schedule stays a candidate forever: without an
advancing cursor a driver would be handed the same page for eternity and
never reach the rest of the workspace.

One row beyond the limit is fetched and discarded, so nextCursor is non-null
only when another candidate genuinely exists rather than whenever a page
happens to be full. Without it every run ended on a query returning nothing.

The SQL is hand-written because an anti-join against an aggregate over
another table is not expressible through the query builder. It goes through
`frontSequelize.query`, which means it carries an effective `noRawSql`
suppression stating why, rather than evading the rule through the form of
its invocation.

Two filters are duplicated in SQL deliberately — status = 'active' and the
mention cutoff — because filtering early is what keeps the caller from
re-reading state for every agent in the workspace. Both are kept broader or
equal to the domain rule and neither touches triggers, so policy.ts stays
the authority and a divergence between them can only cost a missed archive,
never a wrong one. Agents created after the cutoff are excluded too: an
agent built today has no mention and would otherwise be archived tonight,
and the threshold measures disuse rather than youth.

Adds 15 tests over the query and the use case, plus MentionFactory and
AgentConfigurationFactory.setCreatedAtForTest, which backdates through raw
SQL because Sequelize suppresses explicitly-provided values for managed
timestamp fields.

[front] feat: preview and archive a workspace's unused agents (#30976)

Adds the two endpoints and the workspace setting behind the
`archive_inactive_agents` flag.

- `POST .../archive_inactive/preview` counts what archival would take and
  `POST .../archive_inactive` takes it. Both cover the whole workspace and share
  one body schema, so the dry run and the executor cannot drift.
- `policy.ts` holds the rules as pure functions: an agent is archivable when it
  is active, no enabled schedule drives it, its first version predates the
  cutoff and its last mention does too. The cutoff is truncated to the UTC day,
  so a 02:00 run and a 17:00 preview judge every agent identically.
- `fetchArchivableAgents` answers the whole eligibility question, so the preview
  and the executor read the same rules rather than each holding a copy. The
  executor then goes through `archiveAgentConfiguration`, which keeps trigger
  disabling, wake-up cancellation, editor-group suspension and the
  `agent.archived` audit event on the one path that already owned them.
- `inactiveAgentArchivalThresholdDays` on the workspace carries both whether
  automatic archival is on and how many days, matching the policy's rule that
  with no threshold set nothing is ever archived. Nothing reads it server-side
  yet: this ships the manual endpoints, not the nightly run.
- Seeds a workspace whose answer is known in advance: five agents, two eligible
  and three spared, one of them an agent edited today whose first version is old.

A recently mentioned agent is spared without appearing in
`skippedCountByReason`. The candidates query filters on the same cutoff, so such
an agent never reaches the rules to be counted by them; the rule stays in
`policy.ts` so that one module still states what "inactive" means.

fix(mcp): enforce feature flag when resolving internal MCP server views (#31064)

Feature-flag gating on internal MCP servers was only applied at the
listing and view-provisioning layers, never at the seam that resolves a
view by id and turns it into runnable tools. `fetchByIds` computed the
enabled set but only logged when a server was restricted, returning it
anyway. A leftover or force-created view for a flag-gated server could
therefore be referenced by a custom Skill or an agent action config and
its tools listed and executed with the flag off.

Make `InternalMCPServerInMemoryResource.fetchByIds`/`fetchById` drop
restricted servers by default, with an explicit `includeRestricted`
opt-in threaded through `MCPServerViewResource.baseFetch` and the public
view fetchers. Admin/management surfaces that must display an
installed-but-restricted server (server management route, approvals name
display, poke diagnostics/details, view creation) opt in explicitly.

This closes both entry paths at once: skill creation and agent action
config validation reject restricted views, and run-time skill/agent tool
resolution no longer surfaces their tools. The `includeDeleted` branch of
`baseFetch` is unaffected, so workspace scrubbing keeps working.

Add a regression test asserting a restricted server's view is dropped by
default and surfaced only with `includeRestricted`.

Start the greeting entrance above the line and shorten it (#31096)

* Start the greeting entrance above the line and shorten it

Each word came from 10px below over 420ms with a 70ms stagger, so the line
took ~770ms to settle and read as rising from under its resting position.
Words now fall in from 8px above over 300ms with a 50ms stagger — 550ms for
the whole line, inside the sub-300ms budget per word and the 30-80ms stagger
band for group entrances. Travel shrinks with the duration, hence 8px.

The constant is renamed to GREETING_WORD_ENTER_Y_PX: the value is now a
signed direction rather than a magnitude.

* Rise the greeting words from 6px below

Tuned in the playground: the words keep rising into place rather than
falling in, with less travel than the 10px they started at. Duration and
stagger stay at 300ms/50ms.

* Soften the greeting entrance to a 4px lift over 550ms

Tuned in the playground: with only 4px of travel the motion reads mostly as
a fade, so the longer per-word duration settles rather than drags. Stagger
back to 70ms.

* Smooth out the greeting reveal

Two things were working against the 550ms the entrance is tuned to.

MOTION_EASINGS.emphasized is a quint curve: ~80% of the movement lands in
the first quarter of the duration, so with 4px of travel the lift was over
in ~140ms and the remaining 400ms was opacity crawling to full — words
appeared, then lingered. MOTION_EASINGS.enter (cubic) spreads lift and fade
evenly across the duration so each word settles as one motion.

Framer also keeps the animated transform in the style attribute once a value
settles, leaving every word on its own composited layer with an identity
translate, which renders glyphs slightly softer than the static text around
them. Collapse the resting transform to `none`, the same way AgentInputBar
already does.

Both stay on sparkle's motion tokens: no spring, no new curve, no blur (the
repo has no precedent for any of the three).

* Blur the greeting words in, and leave nothing behind

Tuned in the playground: 2px of blur clearing as each word rises, 280ms per
word on MOTION_EASINGS.move with a 50ms stagger — the line settles in 530ms.

The blur is why this moves from Framer to a CSS keyframe. Framer writes
animated values into the style attribute and keeps them once they settle, so
an animated filter leaves `blur(0px)` on all six words forever. A zero-radius
filter still forces its own composited layer, which switches text to
grayscale antialiasing and renders the greeting slightly softer than the rest
of the page — reintroducing exactly what the previous commit removed for
transforms, and no `transformTemplate` equivalent exists for filters.

A `from`-only keyframe with `animation-fill-mode: backwards` has no such
resting state to leave: `backwards` holds the from-state through the stagger
delay, the animation interpolates toward the element's own base style, and
when it ends the element is plain static text — computed transform `none`,
filter `none`, no layer. Verified in a browser: mid-flight a word reads
opacity 0.51 / translateY 1.94px / blur 0.97px, and settled it reads
transform none / filter none with zero running animations.

The from-values come in as custom properties so all five knobs stay together
in TypeScript, off sparkle's MOTION_EASINGS token. Reduced motion drops the
inline animation entirely, which a class could not do here since an inline
`animation` shorthand would win over `motion-reduce:animate-none`.

* Fix the entrance curve: ease-out, not ease-in-out

MOTION_EASINGS.move is cubic-bezier(0.455, 0.03, 0.515, 0.955), an
ease-in-out built for on-screen moves (reordering, layout shifts) — things
already visible that relocate. An entrance is the opposite: it's arriving,
so it wants an ease-out, all deceleration and no wind-up.

The in-out curve only completes 2% of its motion in the first 28ms (10% of
the 280ms duration) and is barely half done at 140ms, which reads as the lag
that was reported. MOTION_EASINGS.emphasized (ease-out quint) completes 40%
in the same 28ms and 97% by 196ms — the word arrives immediately and eases
into its rest instead of hanging back before starting.

Every other value (4px lift, 2px blur, 280ms, 50ms stagger) is untouched.

* Tune the greeting entrance: 3px blur, 430ms per word

Blur 2px -> 3px, duration 280ms -> 430ms. Y, stagger, and the ease-out quint
curve from the last fix are unchanged.

* Animate the composer and "Chat with..." into the empty-state hero too

Only the greeting words animated on load; the composer and the agent browser
just sat there fully rendered. Order of appearance: text, composer, then
"Chat with...", each playing the same fade + rise + blur entrance as the
greeting words, offset so the hero appears as one flowing wave rather than
three animations waiting on each other.

  - Composer: 6px rise, 3px blur, 280ms, starts 120ms after mount (while the
    text is still animating in).
  - "Chat with...": 8px rise, 3px blur, 280ms, starts 220ms after mount.

The whole hero settles by ~680ms, driven by the greeting (unchanged from the
prior tuning pass) rather than these two, which finish sooner.

The per-word helper is generalized into `heroEntranceStyle`, reused by all
three call sites, and the keyframe is renamed from `greeting-word-in` to
`fade-rise-blur-in` in theme-extras.css to match — it never referenced
"greeting" in its logic, only two custom properties for travel and blur.

AgentBrowserContainer takes the new style through a `style` prop on its own
root element rather than an added wrapper div: that div carries `h-full`,
and its parent here doesn't stretch flex children, so the div's height
depends on a real definite height on the *next* ancestor up (DropzoneContainer's
`h-panel`). A wrapper would sit in between with no explicit height of its
own, turning that h-full into `auto` and changing layout.

Verified in a browser that all three entrances settle to `opacity: 1,
transform: none, filter: none` with zero animations left running - the
same "leaves nothing behind" property already required for the greeting
text, extended here to the composer and the agent browser.

* Widen the gaps between the hero's three entrances

Tuned in the playground: word stagger 50ms -> 70ms, composer delay
120ms -> 160ms, chat-with delay 220ms -> 300ms. Durations and travel
distances are unchanged; only the time between elements grew, so the hero
now settles at 780ms instead of 680ms.

* Start the composer a tad earlier

160ms -> 130ms after mount. Chat-with's delay and every duration are
unchanged.

[front-api] declare openai dependency to avoid resolving a stale hoisted copy (#31288)

front-api's esbuild config externalizes every bare import, so `require("openai")` is resolved at
runtime from `front-api/dist/`: `front-api/node_modules` -> root `node_modules` -> only then
`NODE_PATH` (which `esbuild.dev.ts` sets to `front/node_modules`, but NODE_PATH is a last-resort
fallback and never wins).

Locally, `connectors` depends on `@microsoft/teams-ai`, which pins `openai` at exactly 4.77.4, so
that version ends up in the root `node_modules` and shadows `front/node_modules/openai@6.46.0`.
openai 4.77.4 predates the Responses API, so `client.responses` is undefined and every
OpenAI-Responses call from the dev server threw a TypeError that `classifyStreamError` mapped to
the opaque "Unknown error from OpenAI".

Declaring the dependency in front-api (next to `@anthropic-ai/sdk`, which is there for the same
reason) gives front-api its own copy, pinned to the version front resolves.

[front] fix: remove dead Slack search.messages fallback (#31375)

slackSearch fell back to Slack's search.messages whenever assistant.search.context
threw. That fallback could never succeed: search.messages requires the search:read
scope, which our Slack app is not allowed to request (SlackToolsOAuthProvider only
asks for the granular search:read.* scopes). It always failed with missing_scope,
which handleSlackAuthError classified as an auth failure, so the tool returned a
"Personal authentication required" prompt.

The dominant trigger was rate limiting, not a broken token: 4,956 fallbacks in five
days of prod logs, 4,723 of them HTTP 429 (the rest, 168 missing_scope and 65
token_revoked, are genuine). Re-authenticating grants the same scope set, so users
could reconnect indefinitely and hit the same prompt on the next rate-limited search.

Remove the fallback so errors propagate as themselves, and classify 429 (and the
`ratelimited` body error) as a rate limit: the model gets a retryable message instead
of a bogus auth prompt, and it is untracked so external throttling does not alert.

The fallback was the last reference to search.messages in the tree. Prod logs confirm
assistant.search.context works even for workspaces whose assistant.search.info reports
is_ai_search_enabled: false, so nothing loses search capability.

* LLM stream errors: shared classifier + HTTP-status helpers (OpenAI/Fireworks)

Introduces the shared building blocks for turning any error thrown while
streaming from an LLM provider into a unified `ErrorEvent`, and migrates the
first adapter (OpenAI chat completions, used by Fireworks) onto them. The other
provider adapters follow in a stacked PR.

`classify_stream_error.ts` now exposes three primitives:

- `classifyStreamError` — classifies an untyped transport error by
  machine-stable identity only (`code`/`name` and the cause chain, plus an
  optional SDK-class hint). Free-form messages are never matched. Ambiguous
  failures (socket drop, timeout, abort) stay `errorSource: "unknown"` — a
  dropped socket is not enough to blame the provider.

  (known 4xx -> dust, known 5xx -> provider, unrecognized -> unknown).
- `classificationToErrorEvent` — wraps a classification into the emitted event.

Adapters classify with plain control flow (see `openaiStreamErrorToErrorEvent`):
special cases first, then abort/connection SDK classes, then the typed HTTP
status, then the code/name fallback — no shared dispatcher taking callbacks.

`openai_shared/stream_error.ts` holds the wiring common to every `openai`-SDK
adapter (the SDK error classes and status extraction) plus the host -> provider
name mapping so a Fireworks or xAI failure is not mislabelled "OpenAI".

feat(models): skip degraded models in auto stream resolution (#31137)

* feat(models): take killed models out of rotation

* refactor(models): only skip degraded models in stream resolution

A degraded model is now taken out of the auto streams and nothing else. The
previous version pulled it out of `isModelEnabled`, which took it out of every
path at once: the picker, the agent builder, the fallback lists and the
workspace model catalog. That is more than we want. A stream picks a model on
the user's behalf, so routing around a provider incident is ours to do; a
definitive pick -- an agent configured on a concrete model, or a user
overriding the model from the picker -- is the user's, and answering as a
different model than the one they asked for is worse than running through the
incident.

So `filterEnabledModels`, `isModelEnabled` and `EnabledModelConfigurationType`
go back to what they were, and `resolveStreamModel` takes the degraded set as
an argument: the pool walk skips degraded candidates, and so does the
last-resort large-model fallback, which is just as automatic a pick. Every
caller of `resolveStreamModel` is a stream resolution, so passing the set
explicitly keeps the reach of the switches visible at each call site (and the
function testable).

* feat(models): flag degraded models in the model picker

SWR only revalidated on mount and on reconnect. That was fine while the payload
was a near-static catalog, but it now carries `degradedModelIds` and the stream
resolutions derived from them, and `ModelPicker` mounts with the conversation
page and stays mounted: a tab left open for the afternoon kept the set it was
served at load, whatever an operator flagged since.

in-process cache every minute -- so the staleness was ours alone. Focus
revalidation goes back on, throttled to the same five minutes as the poll that
now covers a tab nobody leaves. SWR pauses polling while the tab is hidden, so
this costs a request per five minutes per *visible* tab, and a degradation
reaches a picker in at most six minutes.

Only what is displayed was ever stale: streams resolve server-side when the
message is sent, so no message was routed to a degraded model in the meantime.

[Poke] Frame function page: contract, source and invocation drill-down (#31729)

* refactor(poke): move sandbox function invocation helpers out of pod_functions

Invocations belong to a SandboxFunctionResource and know nothing about what
owns that function — two Resources already referenced these types from a
pod-named module. Move them to poke/sandbox_functions.ts under owner-neutral
names so Frames can use them without depending on Pod code, and so removing
Pods later stays a pure subtraction.

No behavior change: the helper bodies are unchanged.

* feat(poke): serve Frame function details, source and invocations

Adds the endpoints behind a Frame function page:
  GET frames/:frameId/functions/:functionId          contract + publication
  GET .../source                                     the published bundle
  GET .../invocations[/:invocationId[/actions/...]]  the drill-down

Frames get their own shapes rather than reusing the Pod ones. A Pod
function's fileId is its published bundle while a Frame function's is the
Frame manifest, so the Pod shape would mislead; publicationId identifies a
Frame function's artifact instead. Pods are being retired, so a shared type
would only have to be untangled later.

Two things that are not reuse:
- SandboxFunctionResource.fetchById excludes Frame functions (baseFetch
  defaults includeFrameFunctions to false), so frame lookup needs its own
  static. The fileId filter lives in SQL, and any publication resolves so a
  superseded function can still be inspected.
- A Frame function's bundle lives in GCS under its publication, not on its
  file, hence readFramePublicationFunctionBundle.

Also scopes the Frames list function count regression to the route level,
which was parked when the list shipped.

* feat(poke): add the Frame function page

Frame-owned copies of the Pod function view, source, invocations and MCP
action components, plus their SWR hooks, rather than parameterising the Pod
ones by URL base. Pods are being retired, so shared props would only have to
be untangled; this way removing them is a directory delete.

Three differences the copy could not carry over:
- A Frame function has no bundle file, so the Overview shows its publication
  (flagged when superseded) and bundle sha instead of a file id.
- The Author row is dropped: it repeated the Frame's uploader on every row.
- The MCP server view is no longer a link. That page is addressed by the
  space holding the view, and a Frame is not a space, so the copied link
  would have pointed at a space route with a frame id.

PokeJsonBlock moves to components/poke/sandbox_functions/ — it is genuinely
generic, so Frames reuse it rather than duplicate it, but not from a Pod path.

* refactor(poke): simplify the Frame function layer

Five removals, no behavior change:

- Drop `name` from the Frame function shape. createForFramePublication sets
  `slug: fn.name` and Frames have no app prefix to strip, so slug and name are
  always the same string. That also removes a duplicate table column, a
  duplicate Overview row, and the sandboxFunctionNameFromSlug detour through a
  pod-only notion when building the bundle path.
- Drop FrameFunctionSourceError. Its `not_published` state is unreachable:
  baseFetch discards Frame-function rows whose publicationId is null, so the
  storage error passes straight through and the route maps one 404 instead of
  switching over two.
- Drop fetchFrameFunction, a pure delegation. The middleware calls
  SandboxFunctionResource.fetchByFrameAndId directly, as withProject already
  does with SpaceResource.
- Drop getFrameFunctionDetails, a one-line wrapper. The handler calls the
  Resource serializer, which is where the shape belongs.

Restyle notifications as an inverted, stacking toast (#31460)

* Restyle notifications as an inverted, stacking toast

Match the <Toast.Sonner> spec: the card drops its border and light
background for bg-primary, so it reads as a dark surface in light mode and
a light one in dark mode. Title, description, dismiss control and action
label move onto the primary-* ramp so they invert with it; the drop-shadow
stack is replaced by the single inset highlight from the design, mirrored
to an inset dark edge in dark mode.

Icon colors follow the <Toast> variants in the same Figma page: warning
becomes golden-500 instead of a raw amber, and info becomes the neutral
primary-400 instead of a dark golden that was unreadable on the inverted
surface.

Queued toasts now collapse into a stack with the geometry sonner uses on
its own reference site (https://sonner.emilkowal.ski): three visible, each
peeking 14px above the front one at a further 5% scale down. Sonner only
hides the content of stacked toasts for its own styled toasts, so the card
body fades itself out via the [data-expanded][data-front] attributes,
leaving bare cards peeking and restoring the content when the stack
expands on hover.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Let sonner own the toast entrance

The card was running `animate-in fade-in-0 zoom-in-95` (200ms, ease-out
quint) on top of sonner's own entrance transition (400ms, ease), so every
toast faded twice — computed styles showed the li at opacity 0 while the
card inside it was also at opacity 0 and scale(.95). The visible fade was
the product of two curves neither of them intended, and the zoom fought
the vertical slide it ran against. Dropping the keyframe leaves sonner's
translateY(100%) -> 0 as the single entrance, which is the timing the
library is designed around.

It also removes a keyframe from an element that gets mounted in rapid
succession: keyframes restart from zero when interrupted, transitions
retarget from wherever they are.

The stacked-content fade now uses sonner's exact curve so it stays in step
with the transform it accompanies, and no longer opts out under
prefers-reduced-motion: it is opacity only, with no movement to remove.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Put the toast back on Sparkle's motion tokens

duration-[400ms] and ease-[cubic-bezier(0.25,0.1,0.25,1)] were the only
arbitrary duration and easing values anywhere in sparkle/ or front/ —
everything else uses the bare duration scale and the --ease-* tokens.
duration-400 is already used elsewhere and ease-enter is the token for
content coming into view, which is what this fade is.

dark:shadow-none replaces an inset dark edge that was not in the design and
not in the house pattern: Tooltip is the same bg-primary/text-primary-50
inverted surface and drops the inset entirely in dark mode.

Drops gap={14}: that is already sonner's default, so the prop was a no-op.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Give the toast room to breathe

Padding goes 8px -> 12px, the icon/text gap 4px -> 8px, and title and
description get 2px between them instead of sitting flush. Long copy was
running into the card edges. Width goes 246px -> 264px so the extra padding
comes out of the card rather than the text column, which stays ~216px.

The action button's left inset follows the icon gap: pl-5 -> pl-6.

Also collapses the stack demo from its own story, array and component down
to one extra button on the existing hook story — 49 lines of story diff for
"send three toasts" was not worth it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Use the outline variant for the notification action button

The ghost variant needed a className override to be legible on the inverted
card, and still read as barely-there next to the title. The outline variant
needs no override at all: on the dark light-mode card it renders as a light
chip with dark text, and in dark mode it flips to a dark chip on the light
card. Both directions come from the variant's own dark: rules.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Revert the notification story changes

Leaves the story file exactly as it is on main.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Drop the wrapper div the stack fade did not need

The fade that hides queued toasts' content was on an extra wrapper element,
which re-indented the whole card body and made the diff three times larger
than the change. Moving it to the card as [&>*] variants targets the same
elements with no added DOM and no re-indentation.

Also inlines visibleToasts={3} rather than naming a constant used once, and
puts the hello icon back on primary-500: it clears 3:1 on the new surface,
so recolouring it was noise on top of the info/warning fixes the inverted
card actually required.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Colour the toast by outcome instead of inverting the surface

Radja's feedback on the inverted card: it works in light mode, but in dark
mode a large near-white block is too much, and the common pattern is a
green/orange/red surface per outcome, with lighter tints in light mode.

Each type now takes the surface and foreground of its ContentMessage
counterpart, verbatim — success/green, error/red, warning/orange,
info/blue, hello/neutral. Reusing that mapping rather than inventing one
keeps the two status surfaces from drifting apart.

Contrast measured on the rendered output: titles 6.9-15.1 in light and
13.2-19.0 in dark, descriptions 4.66-8.04 and 8.6-12.1. Everything clears
4.5:1, though info and warning descriptions have little room in light mode.

Note this leaves the <Toast.Sonner> Figma spec, which called for the
inverted bg-primary surface.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Add a shadow-overlay elevation token and lift the toast with it

The toast had no shadow at all, only a border, despite floating above the
whole app. --shadow-overlay is defined per theme in tokens.css and
re-exported through theme.css, so it flips with the theme instead of
needing dark: on every consumer.

Light gets a two-layer stack; dark collapses to a faint white ring plus a
deeper ambient cast, because layered shadows do not read against dark
backgrounds. It carries no 1px spread ring: the surfaces that use it draw
their own border, and a ring would double that edge.

Popover, Dialog and Dropdown still use shadow-md/shadow-lg with no dark
handling, so their shadows are invisible in dark mode. Left alone here.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Point Storybook's canvas and story block at the theme's own surfaces

The preview decorator hardcoded #000000/#ffffff, so dark mode judged every
story against pure black rather than the app's background. It now follows
--color-app-background, and the docs story block follows
--color-panel-background so it is dark in dark mode.

The CSS lives in a .storybook-only stylesheet, outside the published
package. Storybook's docs theme itself stays light: it is static config,
and re-theming the docs chrome is out of scope here.

feat: key the Slack workflow summoning whitelist on spaces (#31667)

* feat: key the Slack workflow summoning whitelist on spaces

The whitelist keyed on group ids, which forced front to resolve spaces to their member groups at
write time and let the slack CLI name any group at all. It now stores the space ids admins
actually pick, in the spaceIds column, and connectors asks front which groups stand for those
spaces at run time. The resolved groups go in the X-Dust-Group-Ids header connectors already
sends, so the auth path is untouched.

A space is represented by its own regular_auto member group, which cannot be attached to another
space, and the Company Space by the workspace global group. That mapping lives in lib/api/spaces
and is exposed to connectors through a system-key-only endpoint.

Rows written before this keep working off their group ids. The migration script records the spaces
those groups stand for, over the workspaces named in a file: reach is preserved, since a group
that can read a space and that space's own member group make the same agents visible. It writes
through the connectors API rather than allowSlackWorkflow, which prepends the Company Space and
would widen a row that never held the global group.

* fix: fail closed when a whitelisted workflow reaches no group

An empty X-Dust-Group-Ids reads as the whole workspace to a system key, so a
workflow whose spaces are all gone would have escalated instead of failing.

Also move the space to member group mapping onto SpaceResource, which owns that
vocabulary, and drop the cached group ids when a workflow's reach is edited.

* refactor: name the space group lookup after the auto group it returns

Drops the one-line listSpaceMemberGroupIds wrapper, the endpoint does the
lookup itself.

* refactor: let the Slack config resource resolve a workflow's group ids

Review feedback: the cached lookup reports failure through Result<> instead of
throwing, and listAutoGroupsForSpaces now asserts the invariants it relied on
(a workspace has a global group, a space has an auto group) rather than
dropping spaces it cannot resolve.

* Don't fail loudly on unattributed Slack/system-key Metronome usage

buildUsageEvents throws when a "user" usage_type event has no userId.
Slack messages authenticate via the connector's system API key and
attribute a userId via a best-effort email match against workspace
membership (attributeUserFromWorkspaceAndEmail), which can legitimately
find no match (e.g. a Slack user without a Dust seat). That crashed
emitMetronomeUsageEventsActivity with no retry policy, so the workflow
retried forever.

Downgrade unattributed "user" usage to "programmatic" when the auth
method isn't session/oauth (which always carry a real Dust user), so
only genuine attribution bugs still hit the guard.

* Resolve Slack usage attribution by origin, not auth method

Replace the auth-method-based downgrade with an explicit,
origin-scoped rule: only "slack" (the one confirmed case, driven by
attributeUserFromWorkspaceAndEmail's best-effort email match) resolves
to programmatic usage when unattributed. Every other origin still
fails loudly on a missing userId, same as before — this narrows the
exception instead of broadening it to any non-session/oauth auth
method.

* Reject Slack messages that can't be attributed to a workspace member

Slack has no authenticated session, so the sender is only ever
identified by a best-effort email match against workspace membership
(attributeUserFromWorkspaceAndEmail). Previously, a failed match let
the message through unattributed, which is what produced the
unattributed "user" usage events fixed in the prior commit.

Bounce the request back instead: reject with workspace_user_not_found
when origin is "slack" and no user could be resolved. The one existing
case where Dust itself intentionally posts an unattributed
Slack-origin message (pod_manager posting into an open Pod on behalf
of a Slack-triggered run, doNotAssociateUser: true) is preserved and
excluded from this check — that path isn't reachable from the public
API (doNotAssociateUser isn't part of the public request schema), so
it can't be used to bypass this gate.

Also map the resulting error to a clear, actionable Slack-facing
message (SlackExternalUserError) instead of the generic "an error
occurred, our team was notified" wording, since this is an expected,
user-actionable outcome rather than a bug.

feat(llm): add the model health recovery workflow and its probe (#31880)

* feat(llm): add the model health recovery workflow and its probe

Second half of the breaker, and inert on its own: nothing starts these
workflows yet, so the worker sits idle until detection lands on top.

A recovery workflow is the degraded state. Its id is derived from the
endpoint, so Temporal's workflow-id uniqueness doubles as cross-pod
dedup and concurrent starts collapse into one run. It holds for ten
minutes on a durable timer, then probes until the endpoint answers.

A probe is one synthetic inference that bypasses `LLM` entirely -- no
Run row, no usage row, no Langfuse trace, no counter write -- so it can
never feed the signal it measures. It resolves on the first token and
returns early to stop the generation. Three sequential probes must pass
before a recovery is declared, so an intermittently serving provider
cannot pass on a lucky burst.

Transitions are logged and counted, nothing is persisted: in this shadow
phase the logs and the matching Datadog series are the whole record of
what the breaker would have done.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* timeouts + probe

* fix(llm): back off between recovery probe rounds and drop continueAsNew

The probe loop had no sleep between failed rounds, justified by a round
costing three sequential provider calls -- but a failing round returns on
its first failed probe, so a fast-refusing endpoint was probed as quickly
as it could say no. The timer now opens every round, serving as both the
initial hold and the backoff.

The run ends after MAX_PROBE_ROUNDS instead of continuing as new, so there
is exactly one run per degradation and its start time is the moment the
endpoint became degraded. launchModelHealthRecovery hands that back, read
off describe() on the already-degraded path.

* feat(llm): close the model health loop with breach detection (#31881)

* feat(llm): close the model health loop with breach detection

The only commit in the stack that changes what the system does.

An endpoint is declared degraded when at least 200 attempts landed in
the five-minute window and the provider-attributed share crossed 20%.
The volume floor is what keeps a handful of failures on a low-traffic
endpoint from tripping it; a real outage routinely sits at 60%.

Detection is driven by the write path rather than a sweep: only an error
can push the ratio over the threshold, so an error write evaluates the
one endpoint it just served, throttled to once per five seconds per pod.
During an outage those writes land hundreds of times a second on the
same endpoint, and evaluating each one would re-read the same window to
learn the same thing.

Nothing is persisted and no traffic is steered away -- declaring an
endpoint degraded starts its recovery workflow and logs the transition.

[front] fix: surface Outlook event categories and recurrence (#31976)

* [front] fix: surface Outlook event categories and recurrence

The Outlook calendar tools never showed an event's category or whether it
was part of a recurring series, even though Graph returns both: no $select
is applied on the calendar path, so the full event resource comes back.

Two separate drops were happening. `categories`, `type` and `seriesMasterId`
were absent from `OutlookEventSchema`, and zod strips undeclared keys, so
they were discarded at parse time. `recurrence` was declared but never read
by `renderOutlookEvent`, which is what the tools actually return, so it was
invisible to the model too.

Declare the missing fields and render categories plus a recurrence line.
`recurrence` moves from `z.any()` to a typed subset of Graph's
patternedRecurrence now that we read it, and stays nullish because Graph
sends `null` on non-recurring events.

Declaring these fields is what makes them reachable, but it also makes them
able to fail the parse, which `z.any()` and undeclared keys never could. A
single event that fails to parse fails the whole `z.array` in listEvents and
the tool then returns no events at all. Since nothing branches on these
fields — they are only rendered — they each get `.catch(undefined)` so an
unanticipated shape costs the field and nothing more.

Rendering the pattern reads only the fields its type gives meaning to. Graph
fills the whole pattern object whatever the type is, so a weekly pattern
still carries `index: "first"` and `dayOfMonth: 0`; rendering `index`
unconditionally would turn "every monday" into "the first monday", and
dropping it turns "the second thursday of every third month" into "every
thursday".

Occurrences returned by /calendarView carry `type` but a null recurrence,
so they report as recurring without a pattern. `seriesMasterId` is rendered
so the agent can fetch the master to get that pattern.

All four calendar tools render through renderOutlookEvent, so this covers
list_events, get_event, create_event and update_event.

* [front] chore: drop the Outlook rendering unit tests

Per review: [TEST1] states our tests are functional and at the endpoint
level, and that unit tests are not desired.

The two invariants they covered are stated as comments next to the code
they constrain: the `.catch(undefined)` on the informational fields, which
keeps one odd event from failing the whole listEvents batch, and the
type-aware reading of the recurrence pattern, since Graph populates the
fields its pattern type does not use.

dsbx db: take a ready sandbox, drop the pod-only paths (#32213)

`dsbx_db.ts` had two shapes for the same commands: a `*OnReadySandbox` one the Frame reconcile uses, and a pod-ensuring wrapper behind it. Pods no longer own sandboxes, so the wrapper's owner is going away. This moves every remaining wrapper-only helper onto the ready-sandbox shape and deletes the pod-only rest.

getDatabaseSchemaOnSandbox, queryDatabaseOnSandbox and deleteDatabaseOnSandbox become getDatabaseSchemaOnReadySandbox, queryDatabaseOnReadySandbox and deleteDatabaseOnReadySandbox, taking the sandbox their caller already has. That matches reconcileDatabaseOnReadySandbox and listDatabasesOnReadySandbox, and it is what lets one ensure cover several databases (see database_reconciliation.ts) instead of one per call. Their bodies were already owner-neutral: the databases directory is shared, and FRAME_DATABASE_NAME_REGEX and POD_DATABASE_NAME_REGEX are both SANDBOX_DATABASE_NAME_REGEX, so the name guard needed nothing.

The query spill dir does move. It pointed at the pod files mount, and a Frame-owned sandbox carries no agent-visible files mount, so oversized results now spill to a non-mounted scratch root. `resultsFile` is still a sandbox path, read back off the same sandbox like the regenerated schema file above it -- scratch space that does not outlive the sandbox.

deletePodDatabaseReplica becomes deleteFrameDatabaseReplica, keyed on getFrameDatabaseReplicaBasePath. It comes along because the two are incoherent apart: deleting live files without wiping the replica means the next cold start restores the database, so the live delete alone would look like it deletes a database and quietly not.

Deleted: reconcileDatabaseFromPodPath and the private pod-ensuring reconcile behind it, plus the reconcile-side prefix helpers in db_naming that only they used. None had a caller.

Nothing here has a caller yet, including before this change. The gap the delete pair is waiting for is real though: reconcileFramePublicationDatabases only ever adds or alters, so a publication that drops a database from its manifest leaves the live file and its replica behind. Wiring that up means publish starts destroying data, which wants its own decision.

Poke: drop the pod sandbox surfaces (#32214)

Three Poke views existed only to inspect or wake a pod-owned sandbox, which is about to stop being a thing.

The pod-databases table on the project page goes with its route, SWR hook and columns. It had no database-backed source: it ran `dsbx db list` against the pod, waking or cold-starting the sandbox to answer, which is exactly the reason it cannot survive the owner kind. That was also the last caller of listDatabasesOnSandbox, so the pod-ensuring list wrapper goes with it -- the ready-sandbox variant the Frame view uses stays.

The Sandbox Status and Sandbox Connect rows go from the space Overview, along with the `sandbox` field on the space-details response that fed them. Only pods ever populated it.

The wake-sandbox plugin goes: there is no pod sandbox left to wake.

Frame sandboxes keep their own Poke surfaces, which are unaffected.

Remove the two Pod functions specific features (#32215)

* dsbx db: take a ready sandbox, drop the pod-only paths

`dsbx_db.ts` had two shapes for the same commands: a `*OnReadySandbox` one the Frame reconcile uses, and a pod-ensuring wrapper behind it. Pods no longer own sandboxes, so the wrapper's owner is going away. This moves every remaining wrapper-only helper onto the ready-sandbox shape and deletes the pod-only rest.

getDatabaseSchemaOnSandbox, queryDatabaseOnSandbox and deleteDatabaseOnSandbox become getDatabaseSchemaOnReadySandbox, queryDatabaseOnReadySandbox and deleteDatabaseOnReadySandbox, taking the sandbox their caller already has. That matches reconcileDatabaseOnReadySandbox and listDatabasesOnReadySandbox, and it is what lets one ensure cover several databases (see database_reconciliation.ts) instead of one per call. Their bodies were already owner-neutral: the databases directory is shared, and FRAME_DATABASE_NAME_REGEX and POD_DATABASE_NAME_REGEX are both SANDBOX_DATABASE_NAME_REGEX, so the name guard needed nothing.

The query spill dir does move. It pointed at the pod files mount, and a Frame-owned sandbox carries no agent-visible files mount, so oversized results now spill to a non-mounted scratch root. `resultsFile` is still a sandbox path, read back off the same sandbox like the regenerated schema file above it -- scratch space that does not outlive the sandbox.

deletePodDatabaseReplica becomes deleteFrameDatabaseReplica, keyed on getFrameDatabaseReplicaBasePath. It comes along because the two are incoherent apart: deleting live files without wiping the replica means the next cold start restores the database, so the live delete alone would look like it deletes a database and quietly not.

Deleted: reconcileDatabaseFromPodPath and the private pod-ensuring reconcile behind it, plus the reconcile-side prefix helpers in db_naming that only they used. None had a caller.

Nothing here has a caller yet, including before this change. The gap the delete pair is waiting for is real though: reconcileFramePublicationDatabases only ever adds or alters, so a publication that drops a database from its manifest leaves the live file and its replica behind. Wiring that up means publish starts destroying data, which wants its own decision.

* Poke: drop the pod sandbox surfaces

Three Poke views existed only to inspect or wake a pod-owned sandbox, which is about to stop being a thing.

The pod-databases table on the project page goes with its route, SWR hook and columns. It had no database-backed source: it ran `dsbx db list` against the pod, waking or cold-starting the sandbox to answer, which is exactly the reason it cannot survive the owner kind. That was also the last caller of listDatabasesOnSandbox, so the pod-ensuring list wrapper goes with it -- the ready-sandbox variant the Frame view uses stays.

The Sandbox Status and Sandbox Connect rows go from the space Overview, along with the `sandbox` field on the space-details response that fed them. Only pods ever populated it.

The wake-sandbox plugin goes: there is no pod sandbox left to wake.

Frame sandboxes keep their own Poke surfaces, which are unaffected.

* Remove the two features whose subject was Pod functions

Both of these can only ever have Pod functions as their subject, and Pod functions are unpublishable and uninvocable: nothing calls SandboxFunctionResource.makeNew, and every .invoke() entry point resolves through resolveSandboxFunctionWithCapability, which is Frames-v2-only.

Publish-time validation of Frame-to-Pod-function references goes: validate_frame_pod_functions.ts, a TypeScript-compiler pass that type-checked callFunction() arguments against the pod's published contracts, plus its four PublishFrameErrorCode entries. pod_function_reference.ts goes with it, so a legacy Frame's bare callFunction name no longer resolves against a Pod app folder -- FrameFunctionReferenceScope keeps its v2 arm and its legacy arm now refuses. normalizeAppPrefix moves to slug.ts, its only remaining consumer.

The Pod restriction-impact warning goes: the dialog that told an editor how many Pod function calls would break if they restricted the Pod. It counted invocations of functions returned by listBySpace, which only ever finds Pod functions, so it would report zero forever. countByUserSince existed for it alone and goes too.

Frames keep their own callFunction resolution and their publish validation, which run on the frameId form.
